item.title: Big Names Flock to Ruby-Red Florida to Sway Voters in Unexpectedly Close Contests
item.description:
Democrats did well in much of the country in the 2022 midterm elections, except for one conspicuous spot: Florida, the once-preeminent battleground that Republicans swept that year in a blowout.

Major Democratic donors and political groups mostly abandoned the state after that. Many had already given up on Florida after losing races for Senate and governor by recount margins in 2018, another otherwise good year for Democrats.

So Republicans notched more wins in 2024.

Much of the same was expected this year. But ruby-red Florida may be starting to look a lighter shade of red.

In the final days of this year’s midterms, big-name politicians from both parties have been making the trek to Florida more than they did in the recent past. On Friday, President Trump held a rally in Fort Myers, a bastion of reliable MAGA voters in his adopted home state. He urged his supporters to turn out in force, as they have in past elections, to cast their ballots for Senator Ashley Moody, who is seeking election after she was appointed to replace Marco Rubio, and for Representative Byron Donalds, who is running for governor.

Both Ms. Moody and Mr. Donalds are favored to win. But some polls have suggested the contests are closer than expected, especially in the governor’s race, which would be striking in a state that Mr. Trump won by 13 percentage points in 2024. Gov. Ron DeSantis won re-election in 2022 by nearly 20 points.

Top Democrats and progressives have started to look at Florida with some interest, despite remaining wary about a state they have repeatedly failed to win this decade.

Former President Bill Clinton campaigned and raised money for David Jolly, the Democratic nominee for governor, in South Florida this week. Last weekend, Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont drew thousands of people to four rallies for State Representative Angie Nixon, the Democratic Senate nominee. Former Vice President Kamala Harris and Senator Chuck Schumer, the Democratic leader, are scheduled to hold virtual events for Ms. Nixon. (Former President Barack Obama has not weighed in on either race.)

Ms. Nixon, a former union organizer, has focused on a grass-roots campaign to turn out Democratic voters who do not usually cast ballots in midterms. Mr. Trump, with his visit, intends to draw out similar low-propensity Republican voters.

The appearances of big-name surrogates, and of Mr. Trump, suggest that both parties are seeing movement among Florida voters that they had not seen in years.

“Floridians are dealing with the consequences of Trump’s failed agenda every single day,” Nikki Fried, the chairwoman of the Florida Democratic Party, told reporters on Thursday. “Everything is more expensive.”

The most competitive races may be down the ballot, where several House districts have become unexpectedly close, according to polls. The Democrats’ campaign arm entered the election cycle targeting three districts; it is now looking at eight of them, though some are reaches.

Republican state lawmakers redrew the congressional map this year to create four additional Republican-leaning districts. Democrats now say they might hold at least two of those districts — and possibly three.

In South Florida, Representative Jared Moskowitz, a Democrat, appears to be leading Scott Singer, a Republican and the former mayor of Boca Raton, in a district that Mr. Trump won by nine points in 2024. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report has shifted that contest away from Republicans, to “Lean Democratic.”

In the Tampa area, Representative Kathy Castor, another Democratic candidate, is running against Mike Beltran, a Republican and former state representative, in a district that Mr. Trump won by 11 points. In a new district that stretches from Broward County west across the Florida peninsula, Pia Dandiya, a Democrat and former high school principal, is running against Casey Askar, a Republican businessman and former Marine. Mr. Trump won that district by 10 points. The Cook Political Report has rated both of those districts “Tossup.”

The unusual dynamics have prompted unexpected activity in other, less competitive races, where Democrats dream of unseating a Republican or two. The main super PAC for House Democrats, called the House Majority PAC, is spending money in the Tampa area against Representative Anna Paulina Luna, a Republican who is facing a challenge from Leela Gray, a retired Army brigadier general. One of the issues the rivals have tussled over is corruption, or perceived corruption, in Congress.

Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic House leader, campaigned last week in the Miami area for Eliott Rodriguez, a Democrat and former television news anchor who is challenging Representative María Elvira Salazar, a Republican. His visit included a stop at a Cuban coffee shop that was later attacked online as sympathizing with socialists. Ms. Salazar has campaigned as an anti-communist.

Republicans say that even if national headwinds eat into their recent victory margins, the party has structural advantages, including robust fund-raising and gerrymandered congressional districts, that are difficult for Democrats to overcome. Crucially, registered Republicans outnumber Democrats in the state by 1.5 million voters.

“We need to turn those people out,” said Evan Power, the Republican Party of Florida chairman. “If we turn them out, we will win.”

item.title: On Trump’s Order, Justice Dept. Seeks to Block Alaska Vote if Republican Loses
item.description:
The Trump administration has asked a federal court to block certification of the Senate election in Alaska if the Republican incumbent narrowly loses, a highly unusual move that signaled an effort to potentially intervene in the outcome.

President Trump made clear on Friday that he had demanded the lawsuit, acknowledging how directly he has harnessed the Justice Department to carry out his wishes. “I’m the one that said do it,” he told reporters.

The Justice Department, in the lawsuit filed in federal court in Alaska on Thursday, argued that confusion over a candidate on the ballot with a name very similar to that of the incumbent, Senator Dan S. Sullivan, could taint the election result.

Polls show that the senator is in a close race against Mary Peltola, a Democrat. However, the four-person ballot also includes Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., and does not list any party registration. The senator’s line on the state ballot describes him as the incumbent.

The administration’s new legal gambit highlights its intensifying efforts to claim authority over the midterm elections, as control of Congress hangs in the balance. Elections are administered by state and local officials, but in recent weeks, the Trump administration has filed lawsuits seeking to alter how states like Alaska and California do so.

David Becker of the Center for Election Innovation & Research, a nonpartisan group that advises election officials, said he could not recall a similar instance in which the federal government had sought to block certification of an election, “and certainly not 11 days before an election.” State officials have already addressed the issue of the candidate with a similar name, he said.

“D.O.J. making this claim this late smells of political interference and is against D.O.J. policy,” Mr. Becker said. “The feds have absolutely no authority to tell Alaska when and how to certify. The state officials are following Alaska state law, as the Constitution requires.” He said he expected the courts to reject the administration’s lawsuit.

For months, Republicans have tried to get the second Mr. Sullivan off the ballot, arguing he is a Democratic plant meant to siphon away key votes in a thinly populated state where the winner could be decided by a narrow margin. Republicans noted the challenger had only recently registered as a Republican; he acknowledged working with a Democratic strategist to get on the ballot; and he had a history of donating to Democratic candidates, including Ms. Peltola.

Nevertheless, in June, the Alaska Supreme Court ruled that the second Mr. Sullivan could appear on the ballot, ahead of the primary.

Democrats have maintained they have no connection to the second Mr. Sullivan, a retired elementary-school teacher living in the small fishing village of Petersburg, southeast of Juneau. And the candidate himself has said that he is running in good faith, as a moderate Republican unhappy with the incumbent senator’s tenure.

“My intention is not to trick people,” he said in an interview in Petersburg in August. “I would hope people are informed enough to know the difference between an incumbent senator and a teacher.” Still, he acknowledged having voted for Democrats, including Ms. Peltola, in recent elections.

The lawsuit, signed by a senior Justice Department official, Stanley Woodward, argues “there is a realistic chance that, even if a majority of Alaskans wish to vote for Senator Sullivan, Daniel J. Sullivan’s presence on the ballot will result in a victory for Peltola.”

To guard against voter confusion, the suit argues, Alaska should “not certify any election result that may be impacted by voter confusion.” The possibility of such confusion exists, the suit continued, if “(1) Senator Sullivan does not win the election; and (2) had all votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan been cast instead for Senator Sullivan and Alaska’s rank-choice process played out accordingly, Senator Sullivan would have won the election.”

Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system allows voters to rank candidates in order of preference, with the tallies used in the event that no candidate secures a majority of the first-choice vote.

Political observers in the state have suggested that system could reduce the impact of a spoiler candidate, because voters who rank both Sullivans would see their votes ultimately go to the incumbent senator, assuming the other Mr. Sullivan is eliminated in an earlier round. But some Republicans have said they fear a scenario where their voters rank only a single Sullivan — and accidentally choose the one from Petersburg — depriving the senator of those votes.

The Trump administration argues that the system could add to confusion in the Senate race, because voters might confuse the Sullivans and rank the candidates in an order different than what they intended.

Mr. Trump has repeatedly attacked ranked-choice voting and criticized the decision to allow the second Mr. Sullivan’s name to remain on the ballot. On Wednesday night, he did so again on social media, writing, “It’s ridiculous that the Court didn’t stop this SCAM.”

Representatives for Alaska’s Division of Elections and the state’s lieutenant governor’s office, which oversees the division, did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The other Mr. Sullivan, of Petersburg, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

A spokesman for Senator Sullivan’s campaign said in a statement that voters would be able to make the distinction between candidates. “We’ll let the D.O.J. complaint run its course,” said the spokesman, Nate Adams. “Alaskans can tell the difference between a Democrat sideshow and Senator Sullivan’s strong record of delivering for Alaska.”

Harry Child, a spokesman for Ms. Peltola, said the Justice Department’s lawsuit was a “despicable political threat to overturn an election” that aimed to “suppress the voices of Alaskans because Sullivan is terrified he’ll lose the seat.”

Alaska’s other Republican senator, Lisa Murkowski, who has often broken with her party to criticize Mr. Trump, also denounced the move. “Alaskans don’t need any help voting for their preferred candidates,” she wrote on social media, adding that the state had “already handled this by clearly distinguishing the candidates on this year’s ballot. The Department of Justice should never have filed this lawsuit.”

The Justice Department lawsuit argues that if the incumbent Republican loses and it appears he might have won but for the other Mr. Sullivan on the ballot, then the vote should not be certified until “an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan and any further procedures or relief this court deems necessary and appropriate.” It is unclear how such an investigation would work, since ballots are cast anonymously.

The 14-page lawsuit is the latest demand from the Trump administration as it tries to assert more control over elections.

This month, the Justice Department sued the State of California over what it says are 20,000 noncitizens registered to vote in the state. Legal experts consider that suit’s chances of success to be small, and a hearing is scheduled for next week.

The administration has made similar claims against other states, and the president has long claimed, despite evidence showing otherwise, that he lost the 2020 election because of mass voter fraud by noncitizens.

Court records and analyses by election experts have shown that illegal voting, including by noncitizens, is exceedingly rare. So far, the second Trump administration has charged about 150 people across the United States with illegal voting or voting registration.

item.title: Here’s What Democrats Plan to Do With Their Power if They Win Back Congress
item.description:
With Democrats increasingly confident they will win control of the House next month and hopeful of a majority in the Senate, party leaders are turning to the next challenge: deciding what they will do with their power if they get it.

For months, they have promised voters they will address an “affordability crisis” they blamed on failed Republican policies, pledging to lower the high cost of groceries, gas and health care. And they have vowed to combat what they say is rampant corruption by President Trump and his administration, though they have shied away from promising an impeachment after their first two efforts to remove him from office failed.

Should they win in November, top House Democrats are planning a shock-and-awe legislative sprint to demonstrate within hours of taking power that they are passing bills to deliver on their promises, including restoring health care subsidies and Medicaid resources and moving to end Mr. Trump’s tariffs and the war with Iran.

They will face steep challenges given that Republicans are all but certain to retain the ability to block legislation in the Senate, where 60 votes are needed to advance major measures. (Democrats would have to make a net gain of 13 Senate seats to win a filibuster-proof majority, something not even the most bullish among them expect to come close to next month.) And Mr. Trump will still have veto power. The president and his advisers are also unlikely to bow to congressional oversight, having stonewalled past efforts by lawmakers to investigate their actions.

But Democrats argue they would be able to use a majority to check the president and roll back some of his worst policies. And they expect their actions to set the conversation for the 2028 presidential campaign.

“While Trump is still president, we’re not going to pass visionary progressive legislation,” Senator Brian Schatz of Hawaii, who is in line to be the No. 2 Democrat next year, said in an interview. “If you give us power, we will in some cases reverse his decisions, stop him from making terrible decisions and in other cases slow him down.”

Here’s what Democrats are planning to do if they win.

Should Democrats prevail next month, Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the New York Democrat and minority leader who would be in line to be speaker, is planning to quickly pass broadly popular bills that unite the Democratic Caucus and would undo Mr. Trump’s most disliked policies.

Mr. Jeffries, according to aides, plans in the first 100 hours to speed legislation to the floor that would:

Reinstate expired Affordable Care Act health care premium subsidies.

Reverse the nearly $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts that were included in the president’s domestic policy law.

Move to end Mr. Trump’s tariffs and restore congressional power over trade policy.

Direct Mr. Trump to end the war in Iran or seek authorization from Congress to continue it.

Democratic leaders believe the measures are all consensus items among their members that are basic enough to bypass time-consuming committee consideration and go straight to the floor. They could be voted on before committees were even set up, and would be all but certain to pass in the House, where a simple majority is needed.

The picture is more complicated in the Senate, where Republicans would still have the ability to filibuster legislation even if Democrats capture the majority.

But some Democrats argue the first batch of bills they have in mind are so broadly popular that they could draw enough G.O.P. support to pass the Senate and make it to Mr. Trump’s desk, where he would face steep political consequences if he vetoed them.

“When Trump looks bad over and over again in public opinion, he chickens out,” said Representative Deborah K. Ross, Democrat of North Carolina, who has been serving on an internal working group giving feedback to Mr. Jeffries on the agenda for next year.

“If we’re passing hugely bipartisan bills that are wildly popular, he has a choice,” Ms. Ross said. “And in the past, he has chosen to not buck public opinion on those things.”

Rahm Emanuel, the former congressman and White House chief of staff who has been advising House Democratic leaders on strategy, said the initial slate of bills would give the party the chance to shape the political agenda.

If Democrats propose popular policies that attract Republican votes, “it’s game on, baby,” said Mr. Emanuel, who is eyeing a presidential run in 2028. “Trump then has to make a decision: Signs it, we win. Vetoes it, we win. The whole strategy is what unites us and divides them.”

Democratic leaders in the Senate see a path to reversing the Medicaid cuts and reductions in nutrition assistance enacted as part of the tax cut law, as well as a bipartisan appetite to pass a serious ban on lawmakers’ trading stocks, which emerged as a major issue on the campaign trail.

But first, they plan to address the war in Iran.

“The first objective is to bring this war to a conclusion,” said Mr. Schatz, who declined to outline exactly what legislative actions the Senate would consider, but said there were a number of ways to do so. “It’s costing regular Americans too much, it’s not working, it’s not making us safer. Everyone knows it, and that should be our No. 1 objective.”

Some Democrats have been discussing the possibility of withholding their votes to fund the war, which would be Congress’s most potent tool to halt it.

Whether or not they make any progress on legislation, Democrats are planning to use their congressional oversight powers aggressively to investigate Mr. Trump and his administration. They have made combating corruption a central plank of their closing midterm campaign message, arguing that it is costing voters money.

“If the president is going to veto our actions, well then in the meantime, we’ll be zeroing in on all of the corruption, which is the true commitment of this administration,” said Representative Jamie Raskin of Maryland, who would be in line to be the chairman of the Judiciary Committee next year if his party were to win power.

He declined to outline his first targets, but he named a few preliminary areas of focus:

The pardon industry that has sprouted up around Mr. Trump.

Potential corruption in public contracting and the awarding of no-bid contracts.

The rivers of cryptocurrency that are flowing into the government and to the Trump family on an anonymous basis.

Mr. Raskin said he expected Trump administration officials to disregard subpoenas. He plans to seek information from whistle-blowers, private entities that have been involved in government shakedowns, political bribes and influence peddling through various slush funds, and other sources of public information.

Democrats are expecting intraparty friction about when and whether to impeach Mr. Trump or any of his cabinet officials, whom they have routinely condemned as corrupt and unfit to serve.

Scarred by their experience with two past impeachments of Mr. Trump that fell flat and emboldened him, they have been hesitant to participate in a replay. They are aware that any action that looks overtly political can rebound the president’s approval numbers by making him a martyr to his supporters.

“We haven’t ruled anything in, and we haven’t ruled anything out,” Mr. Jeffries has said repeatedly when pressed on the subject.

But they are under pressure from a large share of their voters to take that action. More than 70 Democratic lawmakers have called for either Mr. Trump’s impeachment or the invocation of the 25th Amendment to remove him.

“We understand from our own experience that impeachment is no panacea,” Mr. Raskin said, noting that it is unlikely that Democrats would be able to persuade the requisite two-thirds of the Senate needed to convict and remove him. “We are sober about the constitutional arithmetic.”

Beyond their initial sprint, Democrats have yet to agree on a full slate of policies they would pursue with a majority. People familiar with their plans say leaders intend to take some action to make ICE more accountable, as well as on legislation to raise the minimum wage and ban congressional stock trading.

In interviews, Mr. Jeffries has indicated that he would look to use the tax code to address high living costs. He would seek to expand the low-income housing tax credit for companies that build affordable housing, as well as refundable tax credits — those available to people who earn too little to owe income taxes — including the child tax credit and the earned-income tax credit.

Democrats would most likely have to grapple with how to regulate artificial intelligence, which has become a major political issue. And they will have to decide whether they want to use spending bills to try to force policy changes on the Trump administration, knowing that doing so could result in a government shutdown fight.

Different factions are also vying to shape the agenda:

The Democratic Women’s Caucus wants to focus on child care and elder care issues.

Democratic socialist candidates have campaigned on Medicare for All and abolishing ICE.

Senator Andy Kim, Democrat of New Jersey, has been pushing to position his “Medikids” legislation — which would provide universal health insurance to children — as the party’s marquee health care bill. “Who is going to look us in the eye and say they don’t want to give health care to kids?” he said. “We all want universal health care; this is the right first step to get us there.”

Progressives are pushing a “New Affordability Agenda” that addresses narrow issues related to the cost of living, paid for by tax increases on wealthy Americans. “We should pass sick leave; the next week, raise minimum wage; the next week we should pass family leave; the next week we should pass vacation leave,” said Representative Greg Casar of Texas, the chairman of the House Progressive Caucus. “I want us to be passing so much.”

One thing that surprised me while reporting this story was how open Democrats were about what they want to do if they regain power. I expected them to be more guarded, saying, “We have to get through the election first.” Instead, they were willing to talk specifics. To me, that signaled both confidence they can win back the House and a desire to do more on the trail than simply blame Republicans for bad policies.

But it also made me wonder how much harder these plans might be to accomplish than they appear on paper, given the divisions within the party — and how much any of this will resonate with voters if Democrats can't actually turn their plans into law.

item.title: Two Former F.B.I. Officials Charged With False Statements About Biden’s Son
item.description:
The Justice Department on Friday accused two former F.B.I. officials of lying to Congress, saying that in testimony three years ago, they falsely minimized their work on investigations involving Hunter Biden, the son of the former president.

The charges against the two former officials, Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, were an escalation of the Trump administration’s efforts to go after the law enforcement and intelligence personnel who cast doubt on unsubstantiated claims that Joseph R. Biden Jr. engaged in corrupt dealings in Ukraine. Those allegations, which have long obsessed President Trump and his supporters, were at the center of his first impeachment in 2019 and re-emerged late in his 2020 presidential campaign.

Both Ms. Floris and Mr. Benavides served on the F.B.I.’s Foreign Influence Task Force, a group created after Russia interfered in the 2016 election. It helped intelligence agencies monitor clandestine efforts by foreign governments to manipulate American politics, including by issuing warnings about covert foreign meddling to politicians and social media companies.

Allies of Mr. Trump have long criticized the task force — which was shut down by his second administration — because of the crucial role it played in undermining a narrative that Republicans seized on to strengthen Mr. Trump’s prospects in 2020. Members of the task force relayed warnings from the intelligence community about a covert Russian disinformation operation aimed at helping Mr. Trump win re-election by amplifying claims that Mr. Biden had engaged in corrupt dealings in Ukraine, where his son held a board seat on an energy firm.

The charges against Ms. Floris and Mr. Benavides, lodged in a 27-page criminal complaint filed in Federal District Court in Washington, were narrow, centering on a single count each of lying to Congress during testimony they provided to the House Judiciary Committee. But the Justice Department used the complaint to unspool a lengthy narrative that bolstered grievances that Mr. Trump has clung to for years — that the F.B.I. tried to undercut and suppress claims about purported Biden corruption in Ukraine.

Complaints are approved by a federal magistrate judge, but are not presented for a vote to a grand jury. If there is no quick plea deal, prosecutors must seek an indictment within 30 days. Typically, a case filed in Washington would be handled by the local U.S. attorney’s office, but in an unusual move, this one appeared to have been assigned to a prosecutor brought in from Kansas City.

At a hearing on Friday, Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui said it was strange that prosecutors had not sought an indictment in the case. The judge set another hearing for Tuesday where prosecutors will have to lay out evidence showing there was probable cause to bring the charges.

After Republicans took control of the House committee in 2023, they opened a wide-ranging inquiry intended to address several of Mr. Trump’s grievances as the 2024 election drew near. Among its points of focus were the warnings by the Foreign Influence Task Force about claims of Biden corruption emanating from Ukraine and a separate but related controversy over a New York Post article published in October 2020 about files it said were taken from a laptop that Hunter Biden had left at a computer repair shop.

The criminal complaint cited excerpts from the testimony of Ms. Floris and Mr. Benavides in which the two disclaimed knowledge of — and involvement in — various internal F.B.I. discussions related to Hunter Biden. Those denials, prosecutors said, contradicted internal bureau messages in which the two officials appeared to discuss matters involving the younger Mr. Biden in some detail.

“Individually and collectively, these false statements allowed her to escape further questioning from a skeptical committee about the then-president’s son in the lead-up to the 2024 election,” the complaint said of Ms. Floris. “These knowing, willful, and materially false statements hindered a duly convened congressional committee from exercising oversight of the executive branch.”

Margaret Donovan, a lawyer for Ms. Floris, criticized the charges, saying in a statement on Friday that her client was “a patriot” who had served the country for nearly two decades.

“The D.O.J. has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts,” Ms. Donovan said. “It’s no coincidence the government is filing these nonsense charges now, years later, on the eve of an election.”

Ronald S. Safer, a lawyer for Mr. Benavides, said that his client had 20 years protecting the public against “agents of foreign governments.”

“In return,” Mr. Safer said, “the government that he loves brought baseless criminal charges against him in a transparently political complaint.”

But Kash Patel, the F.B.I. director and a trusted Trump loyalist, denounced the two former officials in his own statement.

“Lying to Congress by senior FBI officials strikes at the heart of our system,” Mr. Patel said. “No one is above the law.”

The controversy surrounding the Biden family stems in large part from a false narrative that in December 2015, while serving as vice president, the elder Mr. Biden pushed the Ukrainian government to fire one of its prosecutors in an effort to help an energy company that Hunter Biden worked for — perhaps even in exchange for a bribe.

In reality, an investigation into the company, Burisma, by the office of the Ukrainian prosecutor had stalled at the time. The prosecutor was widely seen as an obstacle to anti-corruption efforts in Ukraine, and replacing him with a more effective lead investigator was a policy goal of the Obama administration and shared by other Western governments.

The baseless claims about the elder Mr. Biden’s motivations in pushing to fire the prosecutor were at the center of the first impeachment of Mr. Trump in 2019. After Senate Republicans acquitted him in early 2020, two allies — Senators Ron Johnson of Wisconsin and Charles E. Grassley of Iowa — kept pursuing their own investigation, aiming to issue a report before that year’s election.

The F.B.I.’s Foreign Influence Task Force, however, warned the lawmakers that their inquiry was being targeted by a covert Russian intelligence operation aimed at amplifying the Biden-Ukraine corruption narrative before the election.

Ms. Floris and Mr. Benavides briefed each lawmaker in August 2020. After the existence of that briefing leaked, Mr. Grassley and Mr. Johnson expressed outrage, accusing the F.B.I. of colluding with Democrats trying to discredit their work. Their report, issued in September 2020, rehashed Hunter Biden’s foreign business dealings, but did not accuse the elder Mr. Biden of corruption.

The next month, however, related issues flared again when the New York Post published an article about files it said came from a laptop abandoned by Hunter Biden. Some of the files cited in the article included salacious images of Hunter Biden during a period of drug addiction. Others made reference to Burisma, though none of the materials proved corruption by the elder Mr. Biden.

Republicans have long been angry at the response to the Post article. The Foreign Influence Task Force had earlier warned social media companies to be on the lookout for Russian disinformation operations equivalent to the dumping of stolen Democratic emails in October 2016, and the companies leaped to the conclusion that the files were what they had been warned about and temporarily suppressed posts and links about the article.

The F.B.I. had, in fact, taken custody of Hunter Biden’s laptop, and the task force did not tell the social media companies that the Post article might not be at issue. F.B.I. officials have said they could not have confirmed that whatever files The Post had obtained were all authentic to vouch for them.

The complaint quoted emails showing that Ms. Floris circulated the senators’ September 2020 report to Mr. Benavides, and that both discussed the Post article the next month. But when the House Judiciary Committee asked them about those matters in 2023, Ms. Floris denied knowledge of what was in the report and both played down any involvement in the F.B.I.’s response to the article.

item.title: Trump Advisers Give Fees Earned for Aiding Pro-Russian Government to His Library
item.description:
Two of President Trump’s top political operatives donated the fees they earned for advising a pro-Russian Balkan government to his presidential library fund.

James Blair and Chris LaCivita confirmed in social media posts on Thursday that they made the donations. The revelation came more than two weeks after their work for Republika Srpska had provoked Mr. Trump’s ire.

“I love the President and am eternally grateful for the opportunities he has provided me,” Mr. Blair wrote in a post. “Contributing to the preservation of his legacy of greatness is my honor!”

Mr. LaCivita wrote in a separate post that the donation was “a no brainer!”

Mr. Trump suggested to reporters on Friday that he did not ask the men to make the donations.

“They took the money and they gave it to essentially a charity,” he said, adding, “I think it was a very nice thing to do.”

He said that he was not looking into whether the engagement, which involved traveling to Srpska this month, was appropriate or a conflict of interest.

Mr. Blair and Mr. LaCivita did not respond to questions about the donations, which were revealed by The New York Post on Thursday.

The committee raising money for the library, for which Mr. Trump and his allies are seeking $1 billion, did not respond to a request for comment.

Asked about the donations, the White House referred to Mr. Trump’s comments to reporters on Friday.

Mr. Blair, a former Trump campaign and White House official who runs a Trump-backed super PAC seeking to boost Republicans in the midterms, recently has been spotted traveling with the president to rallies for the party’s candidates.

The two have discussed campaign strategy in recent days, according to a person familiar with the matter, who discussed private conversations on the condition of anonymity.

Their relationship seemed to be in jeopardy after The New York Times revealed earlier this month that Mr. Blair and Mr. LaCivita had traveled to Srpska to advise the government around elections there. They were paid hundreds of thousands of dollars each by the Washington law firm Boies Schiller Flexner, which has represented Srpska, for the engagement.

“If there’s a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!” the president wrote on social media in response to the Times article.

Republika Srpska is controlled by a pro-Russian party whose leader was put under sanctions by the United States government for years — including during the first Trump administration — for undermining the Dayton Accords peace agreement.

After an expensive influence campaign through which the Srpska government paid several allies of Mr. Trump, his administration lifted the sanctions late last year.

item.title: The Financial Woes of a MAGA Bank Entangle 2 G.O.P. Candidates
item.description:
GloriFi was billed as an “anti-woke” bank, emerging in 2022 as a financial hub for MAGA-leaning Americans.

With plans to market credit cards made out of the same metal used for shell casings, the company had the backing of a who’s who of right-wing billionaires. Major investors included Peter Thiel, Ken Griffin and Jeff Sprecher, as well as two Republicans now vying to be governors, Vivek Ramaswamy in Ohio and Rick Jackson in Georgia.

The glory did not last.

GloriFi swiftly imploded, filing for bankruptcy in 2023 only a few months after its website launched. Amid an avalanche of litigation, accusations and aggrieved creditors, Mr. Jackson saw an opportunity. He poured millions more last year into what remained of the defunct company, seizing on an audacious plan to turn his GloriFi bet into a winner by positioning himself at the center of an ongoing legal clash of more than half a dozen Republican billionaires.

Now, Mr. Jackson has been deciding who gets sued, and who doesn’t, in a sprawling bankruptcy court battle in Texas involving scores of creditors. The court fight has stayed off the radar in the Georgia governor’s race, where recent polls have him deadlocked with Keisha Lance Bottoms, the Democratic former mayor of Atlanta. But it has the potential to create an ethical quagmire for a governor.

“Not in a million years would I have allowed anybody in government to maintain this kind of arrangement because of the extreme danger of a conflict” of interest “or the appearance of a conflict,” said Norm Eisen, the White House ethics counsel during the Obama administration. Mr. Eisen reviewed the list of creditors at the request of The Times and noted that some could be seen as susceptible to pressure from a governor.

“It’s one of the craziest things I’ve ever seen,” he added. “You need to completely separate and appoint an independent trustee to manage this. And you screen yourself off so you don’t have an actual conflict or the appearance of a conflict.”

The Jackson campaign, in a statement, said that “in regard to GloriFi and pending litigation, Rick is now supporting legal action because he believes there needs to be accountability for the company’s downfall.”

It would not say whether he would dial back his litigation efforts if he is elected.

The GloriFi legal battle includes well over a dozen overlapping lawsuits, many of which are pending in bankruptcy court in Dallas. These cases are not Mr. Jackson’s only legal entanglement. A prolific litigant, Mr. Jackson, an entrepreneur who lives on an estate called “Le Rêve” north of Atlanta that has its own golf course, has said that he has been deposed at least 25 times.

The Times previously revealed Mr. Jackson’s side enterprise as a movie producer, which also landed him in court. His private investment firm claimed roughly $90 million in tax deductions for four money-losing films, leading to three different court battles with the Internal Revenue Service, two of which are still ongoing. The third case was resolved without penalties after a 2023 trial, though deductions sought by Mr. Jackson’s company were reduced.

His core business is a health-care staffing company that was paid hundreds of millions of dollars by Georgia during the pandemic. This summer, one of its subsidiaries settled for $3 million a federal lawsuit brought by immigrant nurses who claimed they were exploited by the company. (Mr. Jackson’s campaign said he “will not sign new contracts with the state of Georgia and will terminate any existing contracts with the state of Georgia once elected.”)

Mr. Jackson also filed two lawsuits earlier this year against his primary opponent, Burt Jones, Georgia’s lieutenant governor and a stalwart Trump ally. While he has dropped the suits, he still faces a retaliatory $100 million defamation suit brought by Jones Petroleum, a company founded by Mr. Jones’s father. (Mr. Jackson promised to be President Trump’s “favorite governor” during a joint appearance earlier this year.)

GloriFi was spawned in the immediate aftermath of the first Trump administration, aimed at “people focused on faith, freedom and free enterprise that felt left behind and ignored by liberal Wall Street companies,” according to court filings.

The founder, Toby Neugebauer, a Texas billionaire and Republican donor, worked with Nick Ayers, Mike Pence’s former chief of staff, to assemble investors. Popular podcaster and conspiracy theorist Candace Owens was brought on to help pitch the product.

Their thinking was that GloriFi would welcome customers shunned by conventional banks and reject the environmental, social and governance principles that became popular investing yardsticks on Wall Street. But it was quickly beset by infighting, its stumbles amplified by a critical Wall Street Journal story. When the company filed for bankruptcy protection in February 2023, it had about $600,000 in assets against roughly $40 million in liabilities.

Mr. Jackson, in 2024 testimony in one of the lawsuits, expressed regret at not initially “doing a better job of doing my homework.”

“I don’t blame anybody else for me losing money on this deal,” he said. “I blame me.”

But he saw a path forward. Having already invested roughly $5 million, he bought a $5 million stake held by Mr. Griffin’s hedge fund, Citadel, for just $100, before GloriFi filed for bankruptcy. Then he spent another $6.1 million in 2025, outbidding Mr. Neugebauer, the founder, for the right to direct the estate’s litigation strategy and a substantial percentage of any court winnings.

A trustee aligned with Mr. Jackson sued Mr. Neugebauer, GloriFi’s law firms and its former vendors. A $1.7 billion suit against one of GloriFi’s law firms, Winston & Strawn (now Winston & Taylor), claimed that the firm violated its fiduciary duty to the company by favoring Mr. Neugebauer’s personal demands. The firm has called the suit “a misguided attempt” to “impose unprecedented liability on outside counsel for the start-up’s collapse.”

Mr. Jackson’s chief antagonist is Mr. Neugebauer, who ran GloriFi out of his Texas mansion, which is well known in the area because it is a replica of the White House. (It went on the market for $40 million in 2024.)

Mr. Neugebauer has filed civil racketeering claims in Delaware and Georgia against Mr. Jackson and Mr. Ramaswamy, or their affiliated businesses. Mr. Ramaswamy is described in Mr. Neugebauer’s court filings as GloriFi’s largest outside investor.

Other billionaires caught up in the litigation include Joe Lonsdale, a Trump ally, and Joe Ricketts, the founder of TD Ameritrade and a Republican megadonor. Another litigant is Mr. Sprecher, who chairs the parent company of the New York Stock Exchange and is married to the former Georgia Senator Kelly Loeffler, the head of the Small Business Administration.

Mr. Neugebauer, in a statement, blamed “Mr. Jackson, Mr. Ramaswamy and their billionaire cabal” for “destroying GloriFi.” He said in court filings that they undertook a “blitzkrieg campaign of defamation and disparagement,” undermining GloriFi to benefit rival companies they favored, including Strive, a financial services company founded by Mr. Ramaswamy. Mr. Jackson invested in the company, as did Mr. Neugebauer, who later claimed in one of his lawsuits that he was misled about Strive’s business plan.

A federal bankruptcy court judge halted the racketeering suits brought by Mr. Neugebauer before they got off the ground. The bankruptcy estate trustee, who is working closely with Mr. Jackson, has pushed back hard against many of Mr. Neugebauer’s claims.

Mr. Neugebauer has himself been accused, in litigation from the trustee, of self-dealing and drinking on the job. A former GloriFi chief marketing officer testified that she regularly saw him “microdose” alcohol by adding “rum in a Red Bull or in a Diet Coke,” according to the bankruptcy judge’s account of her testimony. (He was also recently ousted from another company, Fermi America, which develops private electric grids, after a fraying of his close ties with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.)

In his statement to The Times, Mr. Neugebauer did not address a question about alcohol; on the self-dealing claim, in his testimony, he said “they are the ones who were self-dealing.”

The Ramaswamy campaign did not respond to questions submitted by The Times.

The scorecard in the various GloriFi cases can be hard to parse. Mr. Jackson’s side has had victories, while a number of creditors have been supportive of Mr. Neugebauer. The major investors have largely sided with Mr. Jackson; the billionaires beyond Mr. Neugebauer have notably not been among those sued by the estate.

When Mr. Jackson testified under oath in 2024, his appearance had moments of drama. He referred to handwritten notes without initially disclosing it, as required, a move that Judge Michelle V. Larson called “incredibly inappropriate.”

Mr. Jackson did make one thing quite clear, though, when a lawyer asked him about his potential litigation strategy. He was ready to sue.

“To me,” he explained, “everybody is on the potential target list.”

item.title: Appeals Court Backs Trump on Constitutionality of Detentions
item.description:
The Constitution does not guarantee undocumented immigrants a bond hearing when they are detained, a federal appeals court with jurisdiction over some of the largest federal immigration detention centers ruled on Friday.

The ruling closes the main legal avenue that judges in three Southern states have used to free migrants who have filed petitions challenging the legality of their detentions.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, which hears cases originating in Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi, was among the courts that had backed the Trump administration’s claim that federal law allowed it to indefinitely detain undocumented immigrants, even those who had lived and worked in the United States for years.

That policy is a departure from the practices of previous administrations, when such migrants generally had the opportunity to persuade a judge to release them if they were not a flight risk or a danger to the public.

But until earlier this year, some migrants had success arguing that their detentions violated the Fifth Amendment, which requires due process.

District court judges across the country have freed hundreds of migrants, citing the Constitution. The Fifth Circuit in July temporarily blocked the constitutional basis for granting migrant petitions, after agreeing to reconsider the cases of the three men for which it issued a final ruling on Friday.

The Supreme Court has already agreed to consider whether the Trump administration’s indefinite detention policy is permissible under federal law, a question that has divided appellate courts. Friday’s ruling makes it more likely that the Supreme Court addresses whether detained undocumented immigrants have a constitutional right to a bond hearing.

In an opinion from a 10-member majority of the 17 active judges of the Fifth Circuit, Judge Cory T. Wilson, a Trump appointee, wrote that because the three petitioners in the case were still “seeking admission to the United States,” they were not entitled to hearings on due process grounds.

The migrants’ argument that their detention violated the Fifth Amendment’s guarantee to “liberty” was framed at “too high a level of abstraction” and was “doubtful,” because Congress holds the exclusive power to make the rules that govern the border, Judge Wilson added. If the petitioners in the case wanted “to be free from physical restraint in the most abstract sense,” he wrote, “they can do so at any time by agreeing to leave the country.”

The three detainees had come to the United States from Mexico and Honduras, according to legal filings. All have children who are U.S. citizens. They were each detained by ICE following traffic stops. One, Ignacio Sosnava Rodriguez, had been living in the United States for more than 22 years, according to the filings.

One dissent, written by Judge Leslie H. Southwick, a George W. Bush appointee, and joined by five other judges, argued that the majority had “constructed an impenetrable wall between the Constitution and these long-term residents, a wall not designed, recognized or even suggested by the Supreme Court.” Judge Southwick wrote that there was a significant difference between those arriving at the border and longtime residents, and that “the tradition for aliens living in the interior has been release on bond unless the government shows danger or flight risk.”

The intensity of the court’s disagreement spilled over into typography. In a second dissent joined by four other judges, Judge Dana M. Douglas, a Biden appointee, put the words “I respectfully dissent” in boldface. A third dissent, signed by Judge Stephen A. Higginson, an Obama appointee, and joined by five other judges, concludes with the word “dissent” in all capital letters.

James Percival, the top lawyer at the Department of Homeland Security, hailed the ruling on social media as a “big win.”

Brian R. Frazelle, the deputy chief counsel of the Constitutional Accountability Center, which filed friend-of-the-court briefs arguing the petitioners’ side, said in a statement that the ruling was “a sadly predictable result.”

“Fortunately, the Fifth Circuit’s decision won’t be the last word on this subject,” he added.

item.title: ‘I Have to Go In’: Dad Describes Killing Gunman in Oregon School Shooting
item.description:
The father who has been credited with helping to stop a gunman at an elementary school in Bend, Ore., last week described in his first public interview how he pursued the assailant and fatally shot him.

The father, Kaylub Giamanco, a 36-year-old carpenter from Bend, said in an interview with Oregon Public Broadcasting published on Friday that the day of the attack, Oct. 15, started like any other. Mr. Giamanco, who did not respond to messages from The New York Times on Friday, said he woke up, helped his two daughters get ready for picture day, dropped them at Silver Rail Elementary School then drove to a job site.

Mr. Giamanco had packed lunch that day, but had to run into town to buy supplies for the job he was working on, so he called his wife and said he would come home for lunch instead. He asked her to reheat some leftover tacos.

Those choices led him to a fateful moment. As he drove onto Brentwood Avenue, which runs right by Silver Rail, Mr. Giamanco said, he saw a figure in black with a long gun fire twice at a red pickup truck and once into a field. Then he saw the gunman throw his weapon over a fence by the school.

“And that’s when panic flooded into my brain,” he told Oregon Public Broadcasting. Mr. Giamanco opened the center console of his truck, “and just said ‘No, no, no, no, no,’ and I grabbed my gun, and I put the magazine in it, and I racked the action.”

Mr. Giamanco, who the police said had a .40 caliber handgun legally stashed in his truck, drove into the school parking lot. He watched as the gunman, armed with a 12-gauge pump-action shotgun, walked along the school’s exterior.

“I was just in full panic, like, ‘No, there’s children, there’s babies in there,’” he said. “I told my Siri to call 911,” he said, and apologized to the dispatcher as she continued to ask him questions.

“I said, ‘I’m sorry, I have to go in. People are going to die,’” Mr. Giamanco told Oregon Public Broadcasting. Mr. Giamanco hopped over a fence, and crept behind the attacker around a wall-ball court. He heard the assailant fire into the side doors of the school as he blasted his way inside.

“And that’s when I started hearing children pleading for their lives, and then I started hearing gunfire, and I just started army-crawling faster and faster,” he said. “And I told myself, ‘This is probably the last thing that I’m ever going to do.’”

Mr. Giamanco crawled into the school through a window that had been shot out, and peered into a special education classroom, where he saw the attacker — later identified as Griffin J. John II, 16, a former special education student at Silver Rail — wrestling with a teacher.

Mr. John had already killed three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and a 25-year-old teacher, Megan Lambert, in the classroom, the police said. He had also wounded a 7-year-old girl and a 54-year-old teacher. But another teacher — the one Mr. Giamanco saw — had thrown her cellphone at Mr. John and had started wrestling with him in what the police called a heroic confrontation that prevented more bloodshed.

Mr. Giamanco, who grew up hunting birds with his grandfather, prepared his gun.

“At that point, I swung the door out and open, and I stepped in, and I fired,” he said. The teacher and the gunman dropped to the floor, he said. The teacher then ran out of the room, fearing Mr. Giamanco was another attacker, he said.

Mr. Giamanco said he saw Mr. John scrambling for his shotgun and shot him two more times, killing him. A heavily armed police officer arrived moments later.

Mr. Giamanco said he put his gun on the floor, put his hands up and told the officer, “‘We need your help over here right now — please, please, please.’”

Then Mr. Giamanco went back to his truck, unloaded his gun and picked up his phone.

“I call my wife to tell her that I’m not coming home for tacos,” he told Oregon Public Broadcasting. He said he also told her: “I just had to shoot and kill somebody, and that I had to watch him take the lives of children and teachers.”

The police have not identified a motive for the attack. They have said the gunman still had 44 rounds of ammunition when he was killed. In the days since the rampage, Mr. Giamanco said he had been reflecting on the shooting with a heavy mix of emotions.

He said he wanted to meet the families of the victims and “just cry with them and hold them.”

“I want to apologize for not saving their babies,” Mr. Giamanco said, adding that the “gratitude for saving people’s children is awesome. But there’s ones that I didn’t save, and that’s probably the hardest thing for me right now.”

President Trump, Gov. Tina Kotek of Oregon and the Bend police have all praised Mr. Giamanco, saying he helped prevent even more deaths at Silver Rail.

Mr. Giamanco told Oregon Public Broadcasting: “I want to be a hero in this world. It feels like I was meant to be here and do this.” He added: “I’ve always wanted to change the world, but I’ve felt small. You know, I’m just a carpenter from Bend, Oregon.”

item.title: Justice Dept. Suit Reignites a Legal Fight in Alaska
item.description:
The Justice Department’s lawsuit on Thursday asking a federal court to block certification of the Senate race in Alaska if the Republican incumbent narrowly loses has revived a legal fight centered on Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher running for Senate.

The battle, which had been dormant for months before the Justice Department’s move, appeared to reach a conclusion in June, when Alaska’s top court said Dan J. Sullivan could appear on the ballot.

Alaska Republicans had sought to have Dan J. Sullivan, a registered Republican from a remote fishing village, removed from the ballot. They filed a complaint with the state’s Division of Elections and said Democrats had planted him in the race to hurt Senator Dan S. Sullivan, the Republican incumbent, by confusing voters.

The Division of Elections, which is overseen by Alaska’s lieutenant governor, a Republican, had followed through and removed Dan J. Sullivan from the ballot. But a state judge, citing the “Alaska Supreme Court’s well-established presumption in favor of candidate eligibility,” ordered Dan J. Sullivan back onto the ballot. The state Supreme Court upheld the decision.

In August, both Sullivans advanced in the state’s nonpartisan primary. Dan J. Sullivan is not waging a competitive general-election campaign, but Republicans have worried that he could win some votes intended for the senator, helping the Democratic candidate, Mary Peltola, a former representative.

Alaska uses a ranked-choice general-election system, which means any voters confused by the two Sullivans could rank them both before Ms. Peltola. But some Republicans have said they are concerned that some voters may rank only one of the Sullivans, and accidentally choose Dan J. Sullivan.

Ms. Peltola’s campaign has said it did not coordinate with Dan J. Sullivan. He has said that even though he voted for Ms. Peltola when she ran for the House of Representatives in 2022 and 2024, his previous support had no bearing on his decision to run against the incumbent.

In the primary, Senator Dan S. Sullivan trailed Ms. Peltola by about eight percentage points. Dan J. Sullivan won 2.5 percent of the vote, securing the third of four spots on the general-election ballot.

Dan J. Sullivan, who entered the race in May, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Justice Department’s lawsuit, and neither did the Alaska Division of Elections.

President Trump told reporters on Friday that he ordered the Justice Department to file the new lawsuit.

item.title: Corey Lewandowski Always Found His Way Back to Trump. Until Now.
item.description:
Over the years, Corey Lewandowski has had no shortage of rivals in President Trump’s orbit.

Fighting for control of Mr. Trump’s campaigns, Mr. Lewandowski has been at odds with Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law; Paul Manafort, Mr. Trump’s former adviser; and Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff.

But through a combination of one-on-one flattery and fierce defenses of Mr. Trump on television, Mr. Lewandowski has always managed to stay on the president’s good side.

Until now.

The Justice Department has opened a criminal investigation into Mr. Lewandowski over accusations that he profited from his role as a top adviser to the Department of Homeland Security, according to two officials with knowledge of the situation who were granted anonymity to discuss a sensitive matter.

Mr. Trump did not offer a defense of his longtime aide, the man he credits with leading him through primary victories during his first presidential run. But it is a rare example of an ally of Mr. Trump’s being investigated for potential wrongdoing during the president’s second term.

“I want my people to be honest, and if they are not going to be honest they have to be prosecuted,” he said. “If people are not honest, they’re stealing from me.”

The incident is the latest in what has been a tumultuous tenure for Mr. Lewandowski, one that has seen him repeatedly removed from — and then invited back into — the president’s inner circle.

Mr. Lewandowski and his attorney did not respond to requests for comment.

In a statement posted to Mr. Lewandowski’s social media account that spelled Mr. Lewandowski’s last name incorrectly, his lawyer, Adam Trigg, said that Mr. Lewandowski had “not been contacted by the Justice Department regarding any investigation, and he denies any wrongdoing when he was proudly serving his country in a voluntary capacity.”

Mr. Lewandowski first met Mr. Trump in 2014 at a political event in New Hampshire. Months later, the future president invited Mr. Lewandowski, who had never run a presidential campaign, to Trump Tower and offered him the job of campaign manager.

While some associated with the campaign wanted to rein in Mr. Trump’s more aggressive tendencies, Mr. Lewandowski championed the motto “Let Trump be Trump,” encouraging the future president to follow his instincts.

Mr. Lewandowski was fired in June 2016 amid internal friction with other campaign staffers and questions about whether he could bring home a victory against Hillary Clinton, the Democratic candidate. Among those who advocated his dismissal was Mr. Kushner.

During that time, Mr. Lewandowski was charged with battery for grabbing the arm of the reporter Michelle Fields. The charge was later dropped.

Unlike other former aides spurned by Mr. Trump, Mr. Lewandowski did not turn on his former boss. He promptly went on CNN to lavish praise on Mr. Trump. “He’s probably the best speaker that our country has ever seen for a presidential candidate,” Mr. Lewandowski said.

The move did not go unnoticed.

“Corey Lewandowski was great,” Mr. Trump said at a rally shortly thereafter. “I have to tell you, and he’s been very loyal, and he’s been on CNN and he’s really been fighting for me, which is very nice, and I respect that a lot.”

After leaving the campaign, Mr. Lewandowski co-founded consulting and lobbying firms, and always sought to maintain close ties to Mr. Trump.

In 2021, when Trashelle Odom, the former wife of a Trump donor, accused Mr. Lewandowski of battery and harassment at a charity event in Las Vegas, she said Mr. Trump called her to express sympathy and explain that Mr. Lewandowski had been “drunk.”

Mr. Lewandowski resolved the charges through a plea agreement with Las Vegas prosecutors that included completing an impulse-control training course and offering an in-court apology to Ms. Odom.

Mr. Trump’s team briefly distanced itself from Mr. Lewandowski. But soon enough, Mr. Trump welcomed him back into the fold, offering him the role of senior adviser for the 2024 presidential campaign.

“I just like him,” Mr. Trump told New York magazine about Mr. Lewandowski. “Corey’s a character.”

During the 2024 campaign, Mr. Lewandowski clashed with Ms. Wiles and her co-campaign manager, Chris LaCivita, over an audit of television ad spending that was seen by many in Mr. Trump’s orbit as an attempt by Mr. Lewandowski to take over the campaign.

That power struggle, which was won by Ms. Wiles, left Mr. Lewandowski with few allies in Mr. Trump’s inner circle.

But Mr. Lewandowski had a different way into the Trump administration after the president’s victory.

Over the years, Mr. Lewandowski became close with Kristi Noem, the former governor of South Dakota. When Mr. Trump returned to the White House, Mr. Lewandowski began serving as a special government employee and senior adviser to Ms. Noem, who was then the homeland security secretary.

Working with Ms. Noem, he exerted significant influence on department operations and policy, such as by presiding over gatherings in the secretary’s office. The longtime Republican operative used his perch to build an expansive portfolio in which he had wide influence over personnel, contracts and the department’s operations on the ground.

But it was that role that led to his current legal troubles.

First, Mr. Trump ousted Ms. Noem amid scrutiny over department spending and high-profile contracts, including a $220 million advertising campaign, causing Mr. Lewandowski to be out of a job as well.

Then, this week, the Justice Department opened a criminal investigation into Mr. Lewandowski following a referral from the Department of Homeland Security’s inspector general, Joseph Cuffari.

Mr. Cuffari had been appointed by Mr. Trump as the agency’s inspector general in 2019, and survived a mass firing of inspectors general at the start of the second Trump term. He has faced harsh criticism from Democrats while in office, but has recently proved himself one of the more aggressive inspectors general.

Mr. Lewandowski on Friday attacked Mr. Cuffari on social media.

“This guy is a total fraud,” he wrote.

Should Democrats take control of the House after the midterm elections, they are poised to ramp up congressional investigations into the administration, and are pledging to look into Mr. Lewandowski’s actions.

Representative Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the Oversight Committee, has been investigating the sale of a luxury Boeing 737 that was later purchased by Immigration and Customs Enforcement, under the leadership of Ms. Noem and Mr. Lewandowski, for at least $70 million.

“Corey Lewandowski has been under investigation by Oversight Democrats for the corruption at the Department of Homeland Security, and holding him accountable remains one of our top priorities,” Mr. Garcia said. “We welcome the D.O.J.’s investigation, but our work continues.”

Nicholas Nehamas contributed reporting.

item.title: Why Legal Experts See the Justice Dept.’s Alaska Election Challenge as Dubious
item.description:
The Trump administration has filed a lawsuit pre-emptively challenging the certification of Alaska’s Senate election if the Republican candidate narrowly loses. But election law specialists said the litigation lacked any legitimate legal basis.

“It is one of the weakest election lawsuits I’ve ever seen,” said Richard H. Pildes, a New York University law professor who specializes in election issues. “It should have no realistic chance of success in the courts.”

Nevertheless, the lawsuit raised alarms as President Trump has sought to undermine confidence in the election when polls indicate that Republicans are likely to suffer sweeping losses, with control of Congress hanging in the balance. Mr. Trump tried to overturn his loss of the 2020 election, culminating in the Jan. 6, 2021, riot.

Neither the Justice Department nor the associate attorney general, Stanley E. Woodward Jr., who signed the lawsuit with an assistant U.S. attorney based in Anchorage, responded to a request for comment.

Here is a closer look.

Voter confusion.

The litigation centers on an oddity in the four-candidate ballot. The incumbent Republican senator, Dan Sullivan, is being challenged not only by the Democrats’ nominee, former Representative Mary Peltola, but also by a novice candidate with almost the same name: Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.

Voters could mistakenly vote for the other Mr. Sullivan instead of the senator. The lawsuit seeks a judicial order blocking the state from certifying the results if Senator Sullivan loses to Ms. Peltola, but would have won had he received votes cast for the other Mr. Sullivan.

It is possible: Polls suggest that Ms. Peltola is narrowly ahead of Senator Sullivan, with the other Mr. Sullivan pulling single-digit support.

However, Senator Sullivan could still receive votes mistakenly cast for the other Mr. Sullivan because Alaska uses a ranked-choice system.

Under that system, people can rank multiple candidates in order of preference. Votes are tabulated in rounds. Each round, the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated and those votes are reassigned to the voters’ next choice until one candidate has a majority. So if a confused voter picks both Sullivans but puts the “wrong” one first, the senator likely still will end up with that vote.

The lawsuit calls for an investigation, though it does not explain how one would work.

It asks the court to order “an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan and any further procedures or relief this court deems necessary and appropriate to determine what the result would have been absent Daniel J. Sullivan’s inclusion on the ballot.”

None that is obvious, specialists said.

The Constitution empowers states to administer congressional elections unless Congress enacts a statute to alter such rules. Citing the National Voter Registration Act, the lawsuit claimed the department can sue to force the state to fulfill a duty it claims the act imposes on state officials to “protect the integrity of the electoral process.”

But the lawsuit takes that vague phrase out of context. It is part of the act’s preamble, which explains the law’s purpose but does not itself carry any affirmative legal force. And nothing in the act governs the kind of ballot access and certification issues at play in the dispute over the two Sullivans.

“It’s the worst complaint I’ve ever seen,” said Richard L. Hasen, a law professor at the University of California, Los Angeles, who specializes in election issues. “No federal statute gives D.O.J. the right to sue over these things. The Constitution doesn’t give it standing, either.”

Yes.

Carol Beecher, the director of the state’s Division of Elections, initially rejected the other Mr. Sullivan’s application to run for the Senate seat, finding that he was not a good-faith candidate and was trying to confuse or mislead voters. But Mr. Sullivan sued, and a trial court held in June that he could be on the ballot. The Alaska Supreme Court affirmed that ruling.

Yes.

The Division of Elections has listed Senator Sullivan on the ballot as Dan S. Sullivan and identified him as the incumbent officeholder and as a “registered Republican.” The ballot identifies the other candidate as “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.” and does not list any party registration.

“It’s not a great situation, but the division of elections did an admirable job trying to minimize voter confusion,” Derek T. Muller, a University of Notre Dame law professor who specializes in election issues, said in an interview. (On an election law blog, he wrote that the department’s “legal argument is one of the worst ones I’ve ever seen.”)

The lawsuit seems too late — the ballot is already finalized. It also seems premature — the election has not happened yet. Either way, election law specialists said, its legal basis is so thin that it appeared to be more about messaging.

“It’s a press-release litigation,” Professor Muller said. “It is litigation that suggests the Department of Justice is fighting for a Republican senator who is facing a confusion campaign, frankly, from another candidate who entered in this race. But it’s left to the political process at this point. There is just not much for the legal process to do at this stage.”

Professor Hasen said one reason for filing before the election could be that courts have rejected legal challenges brought after elections over issues that could have been raised before them. This could therefore be a “place-holder lawsuit or zombie lawsuit” intended to come back to life after the election if Senator Sullivan loses narrowly — except even then, he said, such a challenge would be for the senator to bring in state court, not for the Justice Department to bring in federal court.

item.title: What to Know About Alaska’s Senate Race
item.description:
The tale of Alaska’s two Dan Sullivans has been an uncanny subplot of the midterms, involving the incumbent Republican senator, Dan S. Sullivan, and a constituent turned long-shot challenger with an almost identical name.

That story is now a really big deal.

In a highly unusual move, President Trump directed the Justice Department to ask a federal court to block the certification of that race if Sullivan, the senator, loses narrowly. His primary rival for the seat is Mary Peltola, a Democrat and a former congresswoman who has led him in several polls.

But Alaska has a complicated ballot, and the Trump administration is arguing that the inclusion of another Republican, Daniel J. Sullivan, merits this unprecedented federal intervention.

The best-known candidates in the race are Sullivan, a first-term senator seeking re-election, and Peltola. But they’re not the only candidates.

Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, which asks voters to list the candidates in order of preference. If no candidate secures a majority of the vote in one round, the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated and their supporters’ ballots are transferred to the next-ranked choice.

This year, the Senate ballot (see it here!) includes a Republican named Gerald L. Heikes, as well as the other Dan Sullivan.

Daniel J. Sullivan is a retired schoolteacher, and Republicans have accused him of entering the race at the behest of Democrats as a spoiler who could siphon votes from the incumbent.

He told my colleague Kellen Browning that he was running of his own volition, figuring his name would give him an “instant megaphone.”

In 2024, Trump won Alaska by 13 percentage points, so the state was hardly anyone’s idea of a major battleground heading into 2026.

But the incumbent Senator Sullivan has found himself in a tough re-election fight — and it’s not because of the guy who shares his name. It’s because Peltola, the Democrat in the race, is an imposing rival.

She is a former member of Congress who won that seat twice in 2022 — first in a special election to fill the vacancy left by the death of Don Young, a Republican, and then again in a regular election that November. Alaska’s small population means it has only one U.S. representative, who has to run statewide.

Peltola lost re-election in 2024 and then jumped into the Senate race early this year. An Alaska Native, she’s a conservative Democrat who supports gun rights and drilling for oil. She’s been accused of being an unforgiving and chaotic boss.

But she has shown strength on the ballot already. In the primary this summer, in which a slew of candidates from different parties competed for the four slots on the general election ballot, she led the incumbent Sullivan by eight percentage points. (In that race, the other Dan Sullivan won 2.5 percent of the vote.)

They have. As soon as Daniel J. Sullivan entered the race, Republicans swiftly filed complaints with the state’s Division of Elections, arguing that he had not filed to run in “good faith” and that he should be removed from the ballot.

Their evidence? Sullivan had only recently registered as a Republican. He seemed to have ties to a Democratic strategist. And it appeared he had donated to Democrats — including Peltola — in the past.

The election agency agreed and kicked Daniel J. Sullivan off the ballot. But a judge reversed that decision, and the state’s highest court upheld that reversal.

Trey Grayson, a Republican and former Kentucky secretary of state, said that whether the second Dan Sullivan could appear on the ballot was a question for the state of Alaska — and that it had already weighed in.

“The states run the elections,” Grayson said. “There are federal laws. They have to be followed. But there doesn’t seem to be anything under federal law that would allow this kind of litigation to succeed.”

Highly. The move, my colleague Devlin Barrett wrote, signals an effort to intervene in the outcome of the election.

David Becker of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, a nonpartisan group that advises election officials, said he could not recall a similar instance in which the federal government had sought to block certification of an election, “and certainly not 11 days before an election.”

“D.O.J. making this claim this late smells of political interference and is against D.O.J. policy,” Becker said.
