item.title: In U.S. Gas Talks With Kremlin, Hidden Financing for Alaska Project Emerges
item.description:
At first blush, the proposed venture looks like it would further the Trump administration’s goal of global “energy dominance.”

An American energy company intends to buy Russian technology and use it to access a massive supply of natural gas in Alaska, liquefy it and export it to allies abroad.

The Kremlin and the White House were interested in the idea. President Vladimir V. Putin discussed the plan last month with President Trump’s peace envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, people familiar with the negotiations said, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomacy. It is one of a series of energy deals White House officials believe could help smooth relations with Moscow and eventually pave the way to end the war in Ukraine.

But it turns out that the company was not an all-American affair. The multibillion-dollar project has received secret funding from the same powerful Russian company that was to provide the technology, according to the energy executive who until last month led the U.S. firm and two others involved in company negotiations.

Joel Riddle, who was chief executive of the company, Polar LNG, until he resigned in September, said he had been misled about the sources of the start-up funding, which ostensibly came from a company in the United Arab Emirates.

Instead, Mr. Riddle said he learned, the true source of at least some of Polar LNG’s money was Novatek, a Russian energy giant under partial U.S. sanctions.

“It’s not only unlawful, but it’s not in the U.S. interest to have Russian technology controlling the commercialization of Arctic gas in the North Slope,” Mr. Riddle said in a brief interview.

These previously unreported tensions were also detailed in legal memos that Mr. Riddle attached to his resignation letter, which was reviewed by The New York Times. The memos, prepared by Baker Botts, an international law firm, said the Treasury Department’s sanctions enforcement unit had raised concerns that Polar LNG had ties to Novatek that might present “potential Russia-related sanctions concerns.”

Polar LNG on Friday issued a statement announcing a new acting chief executive, Tim Talkington, and described Mr. Riddle as a “disgruntled former employee.”

But in a statement to The Times, Novatek said on Friday that in fact, it was moving to acquire “minority shareholder” status in the Polar LNG project — a striking effort by the Russian energy giant to seek ownership of American gas production.

The project, if it happens, is a long way off. In addition to the sanctions issues that would have to be negotiated, the technology envisioned is highly complex and must overcome some of the most brutal weather conditions in the United States. It also is competing with another Alaska gas plan that already has the support of the Trump administration. But that the Polar LNG deal is being discussed at all shows how business deals of almost any stripe are on the table during the talks with the Kremlin.

The sequence of events illustrates the unorthodox, opaque mixture of deal-making and high-stakes diplomacy that has defined Mr. Trump’s attempts to end Europe’s bloodiest conflict since World War II.

What you should know about anonymous sources. The Times makes a careful decision any time it shields the identity of a source. The information the source supplies must be newsworthy, credible and give readers genuine insight.

There is no indication that Mr. Witkoff or Mr. Kushner were aware of Polar LNG or its ties to Novatek, even as the broad outlines of the deal came up in their talks with Mr. Putin beginning last year. A U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss the closed-door talks, said that the deal had only been broadly mentioned and that no granular discussions had occurred.

The project, should it ever come to fruition, would doubly help Novatek, one of Russia’s biggest energy companies, first by using Novatek’s technology and second because the company would own an equity stake.

The Alaska gas discussions have taken place alongside talks to sell off part of another Russian energy giant, Lukoil, to the U.S. government and other investors, including some with business ties to Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner, causing consternation among some Washington lawmakers and outraging some of Ukraine’s supporters. The pair have also discussed the possibility of U.S. involvement in future Russian gas exports to Europe. (The administration has said that Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff were guided only by U.S. interests.)

Geoffrey R. Pyatt, who served as an assistant secretary of state for energy resources during the Biden administration, said the idea of bringing Novatek into the high north of Alaska is a terrible one. “It is terrible on environmental grounds, it is a terrible idea on economic and geopolitical grounds, and most importantly this feeds the belief that Putin can get an out-of-jail-free card.”

The efforts to bring Novatek equipment to Alaska have also included a businessman, Gentry Beach, with ties to the Trump family. A college friend of Donald Trump Jr., the president’s eldest son, Mr. Beach served as a finance vice chairman for Mr. Trump’s 2017 inauguration. Mr. Beach said in February that he had held negotiations with Novatek about bringing its natural gas technology to Alaska.

Mr. Beach could not be reached for comment. It was not clear if he remained involved in the project, or whether he was aware of Novatek’s potential ownership stake in Polar LNG.

A spokesman for Donald Trump Jr. said the two men were no longer close, adding that Mr. Trump was not involved in the Polar LNG project. Novatek’s statement said that Mr. Beach had no role in its discussions to take a stake in Polar LNG. The U.S. official said Mr. Beach was not involved in the administration’s discussions related to Novatek.

Mr. Riddle is one of at least three Polar LNG executives who recently resigned. As they departed, Trump officials were notified about their concerns related to the secret Russian financing. Mr. Riddle said the executives had urged administration officials to investigate the matter. The Energy Department, where the warning was sent, did not respond when asked about the matter.

“I felt like I did the right thing to notify authorities at the appropriate time,” Mr. Riddle said.

The Polar LNG plan called for the company to tap into the giant load of natural gas available in the northern reaches of Alaska, a byproduct of extensive oil extraction underway in the region.

Currently, there is no way to move most of the gas that is produced along with the oil, so energy companies inject it back into the earth.

Polar LNG’s proposal calls for it to buy a giant, 640,000-ton concrete-and-steel device from Novatek called a gravity-based structure that would be placed on the seabed just above the northern coast of Alaska, in an area known as Milne Point.

On top of that platform, equipment will be installed that would refrigerate gas supplied by an area oil producer, transforming it into a liquid that can then be loaded onto ships that travel through icy waters and deliver it to customers in Asia.

Novatek uses a similar approach to export natural gas from the Russian Arctic in a project called Arctic LNG 2. Mr. Putin said publicly last year that “we are discussing with our American partners” the possibility of using Novatek technology to produce liquefied natural gas in Alaska.

Korean-made ships with a special ice-breaking design that Polar LNG plans to use were initially built for Novatek, but delivery was stopped by the manufacturer after the United States imposed sanctions on the Arctic LNG 2 project.

From the start, Novatek was slated to supply the gas liquefaction station. But financing for the project was not supposed to come from Russia, according to executives involved in the effort.

Emphasizing the point, Polar LNG features images of the American flag and a bald eagle on its website, boasting that “Polar LNG helps ensure the United States leads,” adding that the project is “America’s Arctic Advantage.”

The company hired lobbyists in Washington and in Alaska to help push the project, according to federal and state records. In Washington alone, the company is spending $380,000 a quarter on lobbying, hiring a former Trump-era Interior Department acting assistant secretary, Adam Suess.

Novatek is already under U.S. sanctions that would require the Treasury Department to issue a license for its equipment to be used in Alaska. Recently passed sanctions legislation named after deceased Senator Lindsey Graham, Republican of South Carolina, makes things even harder: The bill specifically targets Novatek, as well as its Arctic LNG 2 project, because of the company’s ties to Mr. Putin.

However, Mr. Trump temporarily waived the law’s Russia sanctions last week, presenting the move as necessary to keep peace talks going.

During a meeting held at the Four Seasons Hotel in late August in Abu Dhabi between executives of Polar LNG and its parent company, Tech Wave Industrial Projects Management, top executives from Novatek were present. That was when Mr. Riddle began to appreciate that Novatek was directly involved in approving funding to keep the effort going, text messages reviewed by The Times indicate.

Tech Wave is an Abu Dhabi-based company that specializes in managing oil, gas and construction projects. Its chief operating officer is Bjorn Gundersen, who a decade ago was listed in oil industry trade publications as a senior executive at Novatek supervising LNG projects.

A second Tech Wave executive, Ahmed Farghaly, also worked for Novatek until recently. According to his LinkedIn profile, he left around the time the United States first imposed sanctions on one of Novatek’s LNG projects. Mr. Gundersen, Mr. Farghaly and Tech Wave did not respond to requests for comment.

Denis Solovyov, Novatek’s deputy chairman, as well as Leonid Mikhelson, the company’s chief executive, discussed their company providing as much as $15 million to Tech Wave to bankroll Polar LNG, the messages say. Asked about the messages and the Abu Dhabi meeting, Novatek said it could not comment on private correspondence, but that the company and Polar LNG had agreed to “provide each other with open communication.”

“All the necessary decisions were made at the meeting in Abu Dhabi,” Mr. Solovyov wrote in one message to Mr. Riddle sent in early September. “The first 5 million were supposed to arrive by today.”

It was several weeks after this exchange that Mr. Riddle resigned. Two other top Polar LNG executives, Dan Chandra, the company’s chief financial officer, and Jim Smith, a former Exxon Mobil executive who served as Polar LNG’s executive vice president, also have left in recent weeks.

Polar LNG, in a statement Friday, said that “Riddle was recently terminated from the company for cause,” adding: “The company is investigating claims concerning Riddle that may result in litigation.”

But Mr. Riddle resigned six days before the company issued him a letter saying it would terminate his employment immediately, in part because he had raised concerns that some of the company’s actions could be “subject to sanctions,” documents obtained by The Times show.

Questions about the potential ties to Novatek had by late this summer already reached Trump administration officials, according to a memo prepared by an outside law firm for Polar LNG, Baker Botts.

“Concerns regarding a perceived connection to Novatek will likely affect licensing or other regulatory approvals,” Baker Botts wrote in a memo to company executives that was shared with The Times.

In addition, the letter said that federal officials had already made clear in communications with the company that they were concerned that an investor in Polar LNG “has ties to Novatek and may be acting on Novatek’s behalf with respect to the project.”

Paul Luther, a Baker Botts lawyer who worked on the matter, declined on Friday to discuss it further.

Polar LNG would need a series of approvals from the federal government before the deal could move ahead, including a sign-off from the Treasury Department authorizing it to acquire the Novatek seabed platform, given that parts of the company are under sanctions. It would also require a permit from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to build a gas export facility.

Questions have already emerged about whether the Novatek device will function at the planned Milne Point location because of shallow waters there and the “potential disruption to traditional whaling and local opposition, particularly from the local native Alaskan population,” a lawyer for Polar LNG wrote in an internal company memo.

Certain Trump administration officials had already expressed skepticism about the Polar LNG plan, according to internal company documents seen by The Times and interviews with some of the people involved.

Part of the concern is that the Polar LNG project would be pitted against an even more ambitious plan to build a $50 billion, 800-mile natural gas pipeline to move natural gas from the northern slope to the southern coast of Alaska, where it could be more easily shipped out from existing ports there. That plan would also potentially supply Asian markets.

Both the Biden and Trump administrations enthusiastically embraced the gas pipeline project, which Japan and Korea may help finance to increase their reliable supply of natural gas.

“The pipeline makes far more sense,” said Matthew McManus, who until April 2025 served as a deputy director at the State Department’s Bureau of Energy Resources and is now at the National Center for Energy Analytics. “The Polar LNG project would face years of permitting and concerns about ties to Russia.”

Mr. Talkington, Polar LNG’s acting chief executive, said his company sought to seize “a generational opportunity to advance U.S. energy dominance, unlock profound benefits for the state of Alaska, and strengthen American Arctic navigation.”

The fact that discussions are even going on about using Russian equipment — and potentially a Russian-financed company — to move American natural gas to international markets is a further insult to Ukraine, and should not be a part of talks over a possible end to the war, said Ilya Zaslavskiy, a gas industry consultant who previously worked in Moscow and New York who now does research on Russian sanctions and energy issues out of Washington.

“Any approach by Novatek to transfer technology should be seen as a Kremlin attempt to co-opt U.S. policymakers in order to undermine U.S. foreign policy toward Ukraine and our allies,” Mr. Zaslavskiy said.

Rebecca F. Elliott contributed reporting.

item.title: Justice Dept. Demands That California Counties Help Identify Noncitizen Voters
item.description:
The Department of Justice sent letters on Friday to local election officials across California demanding that they help identify potential noncitizens on their voter rolls and set aside their ballots.

The letter — sent to every county in the state, according to a spokesman for the U.S. attorney’s office in Los Angeles — also said local officials would “risk significant federal scrutiny” if they failed to comply with the Justice Department’s demands.

Dispatched a week and a half before the midterm elections, the threat arrived as the Trump administration has begun a blitz of initiatives aimed at unearthing evidence of noncitizen voting or stalling election processes in states where it has dubiously claimed that large numbers of noncitizens were registered to vote or were regularly voting.

Last week, the Trump administration sued California, a heavily Democratic state, seeking to temporarily pre-empt the counting of more than 20,000 mail ballots sent to people it said were suspected of registering to vote for the Nov. 3 election, even though they were not U.S. citizens. A federal judge has scheduled a hearing next week on the lawsuit, but the Justice Department on Friday filed papers urging an appeals court to decide the issue this weekend.

California elections rely heavily on mail voting, which President Trump claims is rife with fraud, even though evidence shows only a handful of one-off cases. The Justice Department claims that California’s practice of sending a ballot to every registered voter could result in voting by noncitizens who are on the voter rolls even though only American citizens can vote in federal elections.

On Friday, Kiersten Pels, a spokeswoman for the Justice Department, said the agency’s request to the local officials is a way to “ensure the most secure election in California history.”

In a news conference in Los Angeles on Monday, federal prosecutors framed the Trump administration’s extraordinary move as a responsible effort to safeguard the election.

“We don’t care who you vote for,” said Craig Missakian, the U.S. attorney for California’s Northern District. “What we care about is making sure that every legitimate vote is counted, that we ensure a level playing field for all Americans.”

California officials, however, have denounced the effort as politically motivated and legally questionable. Critics and judges have said that the Trump administration has generated its lists of names from error-filled data, endangering the rights of eligible voters.

On Monday, federal prosecutors announced that they had charged 28 of the state’s more than 23 million registered voters with allegedly casting ballots illegally in elections. In a separate federal case, a judge in Oakland on Wednesday blocked the Homeland Security Department from carrying out most field operations focused on uncovering voter fraud in nine states, citing issues with the government’s methodology for determining who was eligible to vote.

The letter served on Friday in California says it included a list of people who the Justice Department believes are illegally registered to vote. It describes them as a subset of the 20,000 people throughout California whom the agency identified last week as possible noncitizens who may have received ballots.

The local officials have 48 hours to work with the federal government “to identify who on the accompanying list is a citizen and who is not,” the letter said.

For those whose “citizenship status cannot be confirmed, we request that you immediately instruct the appropriate elections official to segregate — not cancel — those individuals vote-by-mail ballots until their citizenship status can be determined,” the letter said.

Contra Costa County, east of San Francisco, received a letter with an accompanying list of 407 names. But the county will continue to process ballots as normal and has no plans to set any aside, said Dawn Kruger, a spokeswoman for the county’s elections department.

“It’s 11 days from Election Day, and this is just not in line with regular precedents,” she said.

The head of elections in Santa Cruz County said that she received a list with 81 names and that she was still reviewing the information. A letter to San Bernardino County said its list included 1,133 names.

In rural Inyo County, along the Nevada border, the registrar of voters said the list she was sent included just two people, and neither of them had been issued ballots. Danielle Sexton, the registrar, said her records showed they had never voted anywhere in California.

And in Mendocino County, a rugged stretch on the north coast, the registrar said the list she received was completely wrong.

“It’s not our voters that were listed,” said Katrina Bartolomie, the Mendocino clerk-recorder. “It’s from another county.”

In an email sent on Friday to members of the California Association of Clerks and Election Officials, the Los Angeles County registrar, Dean Logan, called the Justice Department dispatch a “posture of intimidation.”

The letter, he wrote, “misrepresents the facts of their own actions, attempts to tarnish the secretary of state and Los Angeles County, and threatens local election officials” days before the election.

But Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Southern California, said the federal government will enforce the law to ensure that only American citizens vote.

“The letters speak for themselves,” he said in a statement. “Any election official who knowingly processes the ballot of a noncitizen is opening themselves to legal jeopardy.”

Devlin Barrett contributed reporting.

item.title: New York Archdiocese Close to Settling Sexual Abuse Claims for Over $800 Million
item.description:
The Archdiocese of New York and plaintiffs’ lawyers were closing in on a settlement on Friday in which the church would pay more than $800 million to settle claims from 1,300 people who said they had been sexually abused by its clergy members and lay leaders.

The plaintiffs’ lawyers said that they had finalized the settlement with the archdiocese and that all of the plaintiffs had signed off on it.

But Joseph Zwilling, a spokesman for the archdiocese, said in an interview on Friday night that the parties were still working to finalize the agreement. “We are not quite there yet,” he said.

Terms of the settlement would call for each plaintiff to have the option of receiving a lump-sum payment of at least $250,000, or a potentially larger payout after a review of the extent of the abuse each plaintiff has claimed, according to the plaintiffs’ lawyers.

The proposal would end a multiyear saga that threatened to bankrupt America’s foremost Roman Catholic archdiocese. The terms of the proposed settlement required that all 1,300 plaintiffs accept it, and there were some holdouts, who argued that the proposal did not do enough to rectify the harms they had experienced. Progress was also stymied by the deaths of some plaintiffs.

“Tonight, we were able to finalize the settlement with the Archdiocese,” Trusha Goffe, an attorney with Jeff Anderson & Associates, wrote Friday in an email to the firm’s nearly 300 clients who say they were abused. “All of the survivors agreed to the revised deal. This means that the settlement you agreed to will move forward.”

Lawyers for the plaintiffs said they had repeatedly warned their clients that if they did not accept the proposal, the archdiocese would most likely declare bankruptcy, reducing the size of any eventual payout and extending the length of the already yearslong litigation.

To appease the handful of plaintiffs who were resistant to the proposal, the lawyers said, the archdiocese negotiated with one of its insurers to increase the amount of money it would pay the holdouts. They would now receive a pot of $20 million to be evenly distributed among them — an uncommon arrangement that hinged largely on the availability of insurance funds.

“The survivors showed an amazing amount of perseverance and patience here,” said Paul Mones, a veteran lawyer whose Los Angeles-based firm represents 33 of the plaintiffs against the archdiocese. “After a lifetime of pain and struggle, they mustered the energy to push that final mile. And hopefully this deal will give them a degree of solace and healing.”

The Archdiocese of New York, which includes Manhattan, the Bronx, Staten Island and a handful of Hudson Valley communities, would be the latest Catholic institution to pay hundreds of millions of dollars to settle claims of sexually abuse.

In June, the Archdiocese of San Francisco agreed to pay $395 million to settle claims from more than 530 people who said clergy members and lay leaders had abused them. In 2024, the Archdiocese of Los Angeles settled similar claims for more than $1 billion — one of the largest sexual abuse settlements in church history.

The agreement with the New York Archdiocese also requires it to publish on its website the names of the clergy members and lay leaders who were credibly accused of sexual abuse, and to keep that list updated with any future substantiated claims of abuse.

The accusers and their lawyers said they thought these requirements would not only illuminate past abuses, but also help to prevent future ones. It is unclear what disclosures, if any, the archdiocese would have faced if it had declared bankruptcy.

In her email, Ms. Goffe said she would have more details about the settlement process in the next two weeks but wanted to emphasize “what an achievement” the agreement represents.

item.title: They Were Accused of Illegal Fishing. They Ended Up in ICE Detention.
item.description:
Standing along the edge of a canal near Fort Lauderdale, Fla., Edguin Morales Aguirre had just cast a line when officers with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission approached him and two of his friends. They spotted a bucket holding egg-bearing blue crabs, which are illegal to have in the state.

After running checks on their IDs, the officers summoned immigration agents to detain Mr. Morales and one of his friends, who were surprised to learn that the officers were working with federal immigration authorities.

“This never used to happen,” Mr. Morales said. “Before, if they caught you fishing in a place you weren’t supposed to, they would just issue you a citation.”

In Republican-led states, officers who hand out fishing licenses, inspect produce and investigate financial crimes have been deputized by Immigration and Customs Enforcement, using their contact with local residents on a day-to-day basis to broaden the reach of President Trump’s mass deportation campaign.

The increased cooperation among states that have embraced Mr. Trump’s immigration agenda is part of a federal program known as 287(g), which pays state and local agencies to assist with immigration enforcement. Once largely reserved for local police and sheriffs’ offices to increase ICE’s access to local jails, it has expanded under Mr. Trump to include unusual agencies like state agriculture departments, gaming commissions, fish and wildlife agencies, and alcohol control offices.

But these agencies have little experience carrying out immigration arrests, which can get contentious and even violent. Some incidents involving ICE officers have led to fatal shootings. Advocates have criticized the enlistment of the agencies, saying it increases the risk of officer misconduct and deepens fears in immigrant communities that people could be detained by seemingly innocuous authorities.

“We have really serious concerns that these state agencies that have traditionally not been accountable to local communities would see themselves as accountable only to ICE’s agenda,” said Naureen Shah, who leads the American Civil Liberties Union’s immigration policy and advocacy work. “What is it about their training that they receive as fish and wildlife regulation experts or agricultural experts that leads ICE to believe it should entrust them with really fraught situations?”

Civil rights advocates have long denounced the 287(g) program, questioning the qualifications of state and local officers for conducting immigration enforcement. Although the federal government previously required several weeks of in-person training, the Trump administration scaled back to 40 hours of virtual training for deputized officers making immigration arrests in their communities.

The Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that those officers “undergo ICE background investigations and clearances.” The department added that it had been having “tremendous success” in making arrests with the help of local law enforcement.

Trump administration officials have urged agencies to sign up, and have called the 287(g) program a “force multiplier.” More than 2,600 agreements have been signed across the country as of late October, up from about 130 at the start of Mr. Trump’s second term.

More than 29,300 state and local officers have been granted the authority to question people about their immigration status and make arrests, according to the Department of Homeland Security. That is nearly five times the number of deportation officers that ICE had before Mr. Trump’s return to office.

The program has become another point of partisan division. Many Democratic-led states, including New York and California, have restricted local law enforcement from cooperating with ICE, drawing the ire of Trump administration officials who say the limits make it harder to arrest people.

Still, the state and local partnerships have become a potent tool for the administration, making up a growing share of ICE arrests, which have hit record highs in recent months. The 287(g) program has also helped Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, achieve his goal of carrying out immigration enforcement in a quieter way.

“We’re still on track pushing as hard as we can,” Mr. Mullin said in a Newsmax interview in May. “We just are doing it in a different way by using local law enforcement to work with us.”

In Louisiana and Mississippi, fish and wildlife departments have similarly partnered with ICE. Even agencies that regulate alcohol and tobacco have signed up in Louisiana and Florida. Nationally, the bulk of immigration arrests are still carried out by ICE, in part because many officers have been deputized in Republican states with fewer immigrants, including West Virginia.

But the partnerships have been especially effective in Florida, which has tallied more than 16,000 arrests through the 287(g) program since August 2025, according to state data. ICE’s most prolific partner in Florida has been the state’s highway safety department, whose troopers have rooted out unauthorized immigrants during traffic stops. The agency has assisted with more than 8,300 immigration arrests.

The state’s fish and wildlife commission has also been one of ICE’s top partners. About 500 federal immigration arrests were made after its officers encountered immigrants, according to state data. The commission referred requests for comment to ICE.

Mr. Morales, a 51-year-old native of Guatemala, said his brush with fish and wildlife officers led to weeks in immigration detention before he was released on bond. He added that he had a pending asylum application at the time of his arrest last year.

Marlene Velazquez Moreno, who was with Mr. Morales when he was arrested, said that she was not detained, because she had a green card. Although she was charged with a misdemeanor, Ms. Velazquez said that someone else unknown to her had left the crabs behind, and that a Broward County judge ultimately dismissed the charge. But she said their friend spent months in immigration detention before he was deported to his native Nicaragua.

In a statement, the Department of Homeland Security said Mr. Morales illegally entered the country and had a prior conviction for driving under the influence. Mr. Morales said the arrest happened more than 15 years ago, and he went to traffic school and paid fines.

Fairuze Sofia, a Fort Lauderdale-based lawyer who represents Ms. Velazquez, said she now regularly hears about immigrants in Florida being arrested by fish and wildlife officers. Another one of her clients, Alfonso Mendoza Perez, is still in immigration detention after he was questioned by them at Lake Okeechobee nearly a year ago. Mr. Mendoza said that he and his brother-in-law frequently caught catfish and tilapia at the popular fishing spot in Central Florida.

“You relax and you catch food for your family,” Mr. Mendoza said in a phone interview from a Mississippi detention facility.

After he was approached by the officers, Mr. Mendoza said he handed over his fishing license, which was valid. But after they checked his driver’s license, he said he was detained on the suspicion that he was in the country illegally. ICE agents later picked him up from the local county jail.

Mr. Mendoza, a native of Mexico, said he lived in Florida for about 17 years and worked as a roofer. Dulce Cruz, his wife, said she and her five children had lost their source of income and now lived in a mobile home with her mother and brothers in South Carolina.

In a statement, the Department of Homeland Security said Mr. Mendoza had been previously arrested for the felony sale of opium drugs. Ms. Cruz denied that her husband had a felony record, and a New York Times search of public records only found traffic-related charges for Mr. Mendoza.

Florida’s agriculture department has also assisted with more than 480 federal immigration arrests, according to state data.

Joshua Chavez, 21, said that he and his father, Mario Chavez Walle, drove to Florida from their hometown in Georgia to sell watermelons at the Jacksonville farmer’s market in late July. They pulled over at one of the state’s agricultural stations to let officers inspect their produce.

According to an incident report from the state’s agriculture department, Mr. Chavez’s father presented his expired Mexican ID to an officer, who then contacted ICE. After ICE confirmed that he had entered the United States illegally, the agriculture officer arrested him and took him to the local jail.

“Undocumented — turned over,” the report says under “offense description.”

Mr. Chavez said the officer questioned them about their immigration statuses, even though he is a U.S. citizen and has a valid driver’s license.

In a statement, the Department of Homeland Security said that Mr. Chavez Walle had been convicted of three D.U.I.s, and had “accepted incentivized departure.” Mr. Chavez disputed that his father agreed to voluntarily depart the country.

The partnerships with ICE have faced intense pushback in local communities across the nation. But some sheriffs said there were clear benefits to signing up. Michael J. Chitwood, the sheriff in Volusia County, Fla., said his office had been awarded $2.7 million in federal funding for making immigration arrests, which it had used to buy new equipment.

He added that officers were not rounding up immigrants, but rather encountering them during their routine work. His officers were scrutinized last year after they arrested a woman who was walking her pug in an area of the beach where dogs were prohibited. After contacting ICE to check her immigration status, the officers detained her, according to an incident report.

Mr. Chitwood noted that sheriffs’ offices in Florida were required to cooperate with ICE under state law, and that the partnership was helping remove some criminals from his community. Although he questioned the need to deport unauthorized immigrants who were not causing trouble, he said his officers were upholding the law.

“If the law says that you should be detained and deported, then we should follow the law,” Mr. Chitwood said.

Sheelagh McNeill and Seamus Hughes contributed research.

item.title: Republicans Aim to Push Trans Issues to Front Burner in Final Days
item.description:
In Iowa’s Third District, a political action committee is circulating a mailer featuring an illustration of Sarah Trone Garriott, a Democrat trying to flip the Republican-held House seat, reading a book titled “Woke Gender Ideology” to school children.

In Ohio, the Republican-aligned Senate Leadership Fund is airing ads asserting that Sherrod Brown, the Democratic candidate for Senate, “supports sex change surgery for kids,” a claim Mr. Brown has dismissed by noting that such surgeries are banned in the state.

And last weekend, Choose Freedom PAC debuted an ad during the Notre Dame-B.Y.U. football game about a “normal guy” who dislikes politics but decides to vote after remembering that Democrats “care more about their pronouns than his paycheck.’’

Two years ago, the tagline “Kamala is for they/them; President Trump is for you” turned into a surprise viral moment. In the midterm elections, the focus on Democratic support for recognizing people according to their self-identified gender has become a staple of the Republican playbook. In the final weeks of the midterm election cycle, Republican campaigns and their supporters across the country are leaning on transgender issues to portray Democrats as radical and out of step.

“The volume is definitely up,’’ said Keenan Crow, director of policy and advocacy for One Iowa, an L.G.B.T.Q. advocacy group. “It seems like it is driven from national groups who have made this a centerpiece and have pushed it all the way down into these local races.”

Transgender advocates say the barrage of attacks on trans issues distort complex questions of medicine, science and law, and encourage anti-trans bigotry. Some Democrats say the approach may backfire in an election when voters consistently talk about economic conditions as among the most pressing issues. Others have sought to deflect the ads, or clarify — and sometimes shift — their positions on trans issues.

Republican strategists note that polls show a majority of Americans oppose transgender athletes in girls’ sports and favor banning gender-related medical treatments like puberty blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy for adolescents. Those issues, they say, are meaningful to their voters and remain effective for mobilizing their base. A research group at Wesleyan University analyzed ads last month for Senate Republican candidates and found that transgender issues were a bigger focus than crime or immigration, accounting for 18 percent of the total.

“The transgender issue may not be a top issue for every voter,’’ said Mike Marinella, a spokesman for the National Republican Congressional Committee, “but once we get up on air with ads that make Democrats’ records clear, voters wake up.’’ The impact of the messaging, he added, can be measured by how many Democrats are responding to the attacks: “When a Democrat goes on air with a response ad, that’s when we know we’ve struck gold.”

Ms. Garriott, the House candidate in Iowa, answered the mailer that targeted her, which included a claim that she voted to “let biological men use the same locker rooms as young girls.” Ms. Garriott ran her own ad, saying that she opposes “men in women’s locker rooms.’’

Mr. Brown, the former senator from Ohio who is aiming to return to the chamber, took a different approach; his campaign’s ad featured a voter who asks, “With everything going on, that’s what they’re talking about?”

Some transgender advocates have criticized both the Republican attack ads and the Democrats’ responses, including cases in which Democrats have seemed to pivot away from earlier support of trans rights. A debate over whether a candidate does or does not “support transgender surgeries on minors,” they say, fails to convey larger realities: that genital surgery is almost never performed on children, and that opposing a bill to ban access to gender treatments for adolescents is not equivalent to supporting surgery for children.

Lost, these advocates say, in the wide discussions of “men in girls’ sports” is a sense of proportion for an issue that, in reality, involves a small number of trans athletes competing against girls and women in the same age bracket.

About 2.8 million people age 13 and older in the United States identify as transgender, according to an analysis of government data by the Williams Institute at U.C.L.A. That amounts to about 1 percent of the population in that age group. In a national poll released earlier this month by A.P.-NORC, 11 percent of adults said transgender issues were a top priority, while 51 percent said they were not important. No other category, including crime, health care or artificial intelligence was found to be unimportant by so many.

Increasingly, the Republicans have leaned into trans issues in recent weeks. Elon Musk’s super PAC this month poured money into targeting Democratic candidates on transgender issues. President Trump used an anti-trans slur in a Truth Social post as he described the Democratic candidate for Senate from South Carolina, Dr. Annie Andrews.

“When you don’t have anything good to run on, you manufacture a distraction and hope no one will notice,’’ said Brian Bond, chief executive of PFLAG, an L.G.B.T.Q. advocacy group.

Even the American Principles Project, a conservative advocacy group that helped to pioneer the strategy of focusing on trans issues to boost Republicans, has concluded that it may not be enough this time. In a memo last month, the group cautioned that Republican candidates “need to both highlight Democrats’ cultural radicalism while also proposing a compelling economic alternative.”

But some Democrats argue that Republican critiques over trans issues resonate because Democrats themselves have often seemed to suggest that support for transgender rights should be a candidate litmus test without building public consensus on the issue. While large majorities of Americans oppose discrimination against transgender people in areas like housing and employment, many also believe that self-identified gender should not replace birth sex as an organizing principle for society when it comes to sports, locker rooms and identity documents.

Since 2020, more than two dozen Republican-led states have passed restrictions on transgender young people. For the first time, ballot measures in this election will ask voters in four states to weigh in on trans sports participation. The results of those measures, including in Democrat-led Washington State and Colorado, will be closely watched as a test for the potency of the issues in the 2028 election cycle. In Missouri, voters will also decide whether to add language to the State Constitution banning gender-transition medical treatments for transgender adolescents.

Strategists who have pushed the Democratic Party to moderate on trans issues say repositioning — even under the pressure from critical ads — can help to mute Republican efforts to paint Democrats as extreme. James Talarico, the Democratic Senate candidate in Texas, for instance, has revised his stance on trans athletes’ playing in girls’ sports as criticism emerged. He told Fox News that he was opposed “if it endangers safety or fairness.”

Some Democrats warn that the party risks alienating its own base by distancing itself from transgender issues, which it has for over a decade held up as a critical civil rights battle. Earlier this week, an audience member at a town-hall-style campaign event for Troy Jackson, the Democratic nominee in Maine’s closely watched Senate race, said that “I and a lot of trans people in America feel that we have been abandoned by the Democratic Party.”

Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, a progressive Democrat considering a 2028 presidential run, said she wanted the audience member to know how “sorry I am that there are people out there that scare so easily after an election.”

But Adam Jentleson, president of the Searchlight Institute, a centrist Democratic think tank, said that it would benefit the broader cause of transgender rights if Democrats aligned themselves with mainstream sentiment on specific elements of trans policies.

“What puts trans people under the most severe threat is when people win elections who don’t believe they exist and want to roll back their rights across the board,” he said, adding, “A better approach is to say: Let’s find a way to protect trans civil rights broadly, and accept that there are areas where we still have some more persuasion to do.”

Efforts at that persuasion have been underway in several of the states where sports and medical restrictions for trans young people are on the ballot next month. A group called Families Not Politics, for instance, has been knocking on doors in several Colorado counties, trying to carry out the sorts of one-on-one, in-depth conversations around trans issues that are credited with having persuaded an initially hostile American public to legalize same-sex marriage in many states in the early 2010s.

The parents of trans young people have been among those stopping at houses as part of the group’s campaign. Some of the parents, the group’s leaders say, describe their own confusion about what it means to be transgender, but also talk about their hopes to help their children play sports and get medical treatments. Uncertain is whether that could be enough to persuade Colorado voters to reject the ballot measures banning trans athletes in girls’ sports and gender-transition surgery for minors.

“This is long work,” said Jax Gonzalez, the group’s political director.

item.title: Beef and Barn Dances: A Farmer Tries to Turn a Red Patch of N.C. Blue
item.description:
A western North Carolina farmer famous for his grass-fed beef approached the microphone this month to the plucking, piercing whirl of a mandolin-led bluegrass band. Voters cheered.

“Hey, everybody,” Jamie Ager, who is also a Democratic House candidate, said to hearty yahoos. The joviality was understandable because, remarkably, Mr. Ager, a fourth-generation farmer with his flannel untucked and jeans faded, has a good shot of flipping a deeply conservative district in the western mountains of the state.

“We snuck up on them a little bit, didn’t we?” Mr. Ager said.

The state’s 11th Congressional District — a forested, river-winding patch of mostly rural counties — was not supposed to be this competitive for Democrats, even with the liberal bubble of Asheville growing. Not since Heath Shuler did it in 2007 has a Democrat won the region, and Mr. Shuler, who went on to serve three terms, was a former star quarterback.

But the race has come to exemplify two defining trends of the 2026 midterms: An unpopular Republican president, coupled with soaring energy prices and an unpopular war, has put rural reaches from Kansas to Virginia back on the political battlefield — and candidate quality still matters.

Mr. Ager is airing an ad showing him barn dancing and proclaiming, “Politicians just dance with the lobbyists, but I’ll take a good mountain hoedown any day.” State Representative Jennifer Balkcom, his Republican opponent, may be best known for a claim her mother made in a TV ad that she had shot someone who tried to break into her home, but some of Ms. Balkcom’s TV appearances have also made her look like a Carolina white-tailed deer caught in the headlights.

The race was turned on its head this summer when a report found that Representative Chuck Edwards, the Republican incumbent, had sexually harassed women on his staff, prompting him to drop out in August.

Mr. Ager may have had a shot against Mr. Edwards. Some professional prognosticators now say Mr. Ager is favored against Ms. Balkcom.

Ms. Balkcom has occasionally stumbled in interviews. In one from Spectrum News, she was asked if Mr. Edwards should resign; she took a 15-second pause before answering, “I’m not sure.” Later in the interview, she was asked what she would do to bring down the prices. Her answer: “I’m not sure yet. I have a couple ideas, but I’m not sure which one I would actually implement yet.”

Ms. Balkcom’s campaign did not respond to multiple requests for an interview.

The main issues driving the race have mirrored those around the country, including the rising costs of living and health care.

But also at stake is the political identity of a largely poor place long wary of government yet in desperate need of its assistance. Hurricane Helene decimated western North Carolina in 2024, killing more than 100 people and causing nearly $60 billion in damages. Federal help has been slow to reach the region.

Both candidates have promised help.

Mr. Ager has a pedigree. His grandfather, James McClure Clarke, a Democrat, represented the district for three House terms in the 1980s. His father, John Ager, served in the State House. His oldest brother, Eric Ager, now serves in that same chamber.

At a rally this month, Vice President JD Vance, who mispronounced Ager (ay-ger) as “ah-ger,” said the Democrat was “born into a political dynasty” and had been handed everything in life.

But Mr. Ager has embraced his lineage. His green campaign signs nod to the ones his grandfather used, as well as the distance he’s keeping from a political party that has struggled to connect with rural voters. He has largely not campaigned with other prominent Democratic politicians since spring, including former Gov. Roy Cooper, who is favored to flip one of the state’s Senate seats.

His candidacy illustrates the tightrope rural Democrats must walk. The progressive crowd in Asheville wishes Mr. Ager would steer left. Some Republican voters and registered independents embrace his middle-of-the-road style; most conservatives just focus on the “D” next to his name.

“To think that a complicated human can be adequately described in a political campaign is just impossible,” Mr. Ager said in an interview at his farm.

For Mr. Ager, soccer at Warren Wilson College was the warm-up to politics.

“I was good, people depended on me, it was fun,” he said. Soccer also involved a lot of flopping, complaining and minimal action.

Mr. Ager was at a cattle sale in Siler City, N.C., last year when his oldest brother called to share that his name kept coming up in Democratic circles as someone who could put up an election fight.

His farm, a leader in the regenerative agriculture movement, which believes in improving the environment and not just sustaining it, was doing well. His three sons were grown. His wife told him he was “too curious not to do this.”

To Democrats, he was a dream rural candidate. He spent his childhood feeding calves. His senior science project involved raising pastured chickens.

Republican ads label him an extreme progressive. They describe his hands-on liberal arts school as a communist-friendly “labor camp.” A new ad, generated by artificial intelligence, features fake footage of Mr. Ager dancing with drag queens.

Brian Mazur, 33, an independent in Bryson City, N.C., was trying to sort it out at an Ager meet-and-greet this month by the Nantahala River, a popular white-water rafting destination. His MAGA-hat-wearing friends were fed up with gas prices. He believed the Democratic Party was still hollow and elitist.

So when Mr. Ager approached, Mr. Mazur, a retired Air Force veteran, asked without hesitation how he would handle pressure from Democratic leaders to vote their way.

“I’m not here to represent some party,” Mr. Ager said, noting that “they might get mad at me, but that’s OK.”

He added, “We’re Americans way before we’re a political party.”

Mr. Mazur responded, “That’s what I came here to hear.”

item.title: She Was Punched After Heckling Trump. No One Has Been Charged.
item.description:
The night before President Trump spoke in Youngstown, Ohio, this month, Blake Miley stayed up past 4 a.m., cutting out felt letters for a T-shirt that would say “RELEASE THE EPSTEIN FILES.”

The next evening, she went to the rally and stood up halfway through, revealing her shirt and yelling, “Fascist, fascist!” Almost immediately, Ms. Miley, 29, was tackled, held down and punched by male rally-goers as the president mocked her from the stage, calling her “scum,” “low-class,” and “a fat guy.”

As Mr. Trump barnstorms the country hoping to revive his base ahead of the midterm election, he is returning to an old habit: heckling protesters and encouraging violence against them. In Georgia last week, he expressed his love for a supporter who had responded to a protester by “slapping the guy around,” and promised to bring the slapper to Washington. In South Carolina on Wednesday, he praised an “incredible” punch that a rally-goer landed on another protester, saying, “He got whacked, man!”

Ten years after Mr. Trump shocked some voters by saying he would personally like to punch a protester in the face at one of his rallies, these skirmishes are now met by many with a shrug. Ms. Miley, who is identifying herself publicly for the first time, said she suspects that no one in power much cares that she got beaten up.

“I knew there was a really good possibility that this would happen,” she said. “But I don’t blame myself. It is not right what they did to me.”

Ms. Miley attended the rally alone, and had intentionally seated herself among people who seemed older, she said. She hoped it would keep her safe. But as soon as she started yelling, a man grabbed for her neck and then shoved her backward, video of the episode shows. When she stood back up, another man appeared to pull her to the ground, put her in a headlock, yank her hair and punch her in the face.

She remembers being hit twice, unable to get up until Mahoning County sheriff’s deputies intervened about 30 seconds into the brawl.

“What he doesn’t know is that his mother and father voted for me,” Mr. Trump continued about Ms. Miley, who is a woman. “Oh, he looks so terrible. And he’s going to get home and he’s going to get smacked.”

The deputies escorted Ms. Miley out of the arena. The men who attacked her were left alone. One raised his fists and high-fived those around him.

In the arena’s parking lot, Ms. Miley was shaking so severely that onlookers called her an ambulance. She said she spent a few hours at the hospital, was discharged, and drove in a daze to her mobile home north of Columbus. She threw her Epstein shirt in her closet and collapsed onto her bed.

Back in Youngstown, the Mahoning County Sheriff’s Department was getting flooded with angry calls from people who had seen video of the incident, demanding to know why no one had been arrested. The sheriff, Jerry Greene, said he had as many 800 phone messages, many of them containing raw abuse.

Video footage, Sheriff Greene said, clearly showed a woman being punched in the face. “I know what people saw, and if I saw that video, too, I’d be like, ‘My God, why didn’t the police do anything?’”

Sheriff Greene, who had changed parties to become a Republican in 2023, said that he is, in fact, doing something. He reviewed body camera footage, which he said shows that his deputies were pushing through the crowd to reach Ms. Miley and did not witness the punch.

He has identified three men who he said took part in the assault, including a New Jersey resident who said in a now-deleted Facebook post that he and two friends had “subdued her and threw her to the concrete.” Investigators believe the other two men, including the one who threw the punch, are local; none could be reached by The Times.

The sheriff said that all three would be interviewed in coming days. He is waiting for medical records from Ms. Miley’s trip to the emergency room, he added, to determine whether her injuries were severe enough to warrant felony charges instead of misdemeanors.

Three days after the rally, one of the sheriff’s investigators tracked down Ms. Miley through her mother, who, contrary to Mr. Trump’s presumption, does not vote.

She had not told her parents she was going to the Trump rally. Though she had been to a few local protests before, facing down the president and his most fervent supporters directly was out of character for Ms. Miley, who spends most of her days at home.

She frequently has seizures, she said, and after years of passing out while working at warehouses, nursing homes and retail stores, she has not held a job since April. Lately, she relies on financial help from her boyfriend, who works in an auto-parts store, and her mother, who is a nurse.

“Most days are quite monotonous for me,” she said. “I get up. I might wash dishes or do laundry. I work on my art.”

When she scrolls, her feeds seem to constantly be filled with news about Mr. Trump and how he is changing the country.

She is worried about the prospect of losing Medicaid, which is likely to happen next year unless she starts working, volunteering or going to school 80 hours per month under a new law that Mr. Trump championed. She is worried about the cost of gas and groceries for her grandparents, who are still working at ages 79 and 82. But Ms. Miley is particularly bothered about the millions of documents related to sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, she said, because of her own experiences with abuse in a past relationship.

She has watched every documentary she can find on Mr. Epstein, who before his arrest and subsequent suicide routinely communicated with politicians, celebrities and business executives — including Mr. Trump. Many of their names appear in the files of documents, some of which the Justice Department started releasing, with redactions, last year after months of resistance from the president.

Most days this year, as she waited for her boyfriend to come home for dinner, Ms. Miley felt as though she could do little about the actions of Mr. Trump. But this month, a video came across her TikTok feed of a protester interrupting a Trump rally in Vandalia, Ohio, and being escorted out.

It was something simple, something doable.

The president, she realized, would be back in her state just a few days later.

She said she did not coordinate with any formal protest group, and despite Mr. Trump’s allegation that she was paid, went on her own accord.

In the days after she came home with cuts on her face and bruises on her arms, she read dozens of posts about the incident. She noticed the commenters who called her brave, who seemed to far outweigh the ones that made fun of her. It bothered her that there were AI-generated images of the scene, but one showed her with her arms raised, her face defiant. “I’m with her,” the caption said.

A high-profile civil rights attorney, Subodh Chandra, tracked her down and is representing her for free. Mr. Chandra said he has been in touch with Sheriff Greene, and he feels “persuaded that they are trying to do their jobs.” If arrests are not made, he said, Ohio has a law allowing citizens to file charges for a judge to review.

Kitty Bennett contributed research.

item.title: Obama Returns to the Trail, Setting Up Dueling Appearances With Trump
item.description:
Former President Barack Obama is hitting the trail on Saturday for his first campaign rallies of the midterm elections, putting him directly counter to President Trump, who is set to speak at a rally in the evening.

Mr. Obama’s return to rally stages in Ohio and Michigan sets up a rare split-screen between him and Mr. Trump, who will appear in Georgia. The two presidents are presenting starkly different pitches on the eve of the midterms, with their parties locked in bitter battles for control of Congress and statehouses.

Mr. Obama is expected to argue that Americans have an opportunity to elevate public servants who will bring accountability to Washington, and to speak about what he sees as abuses of power unfolding in the federal government, according to his representatives. He will also address artificial intelligence, arguing that Democrats are a better choice to address the fast-developing and disruptive technology, his team said.

“President Obama understands the stakes of this election could not be any higher,” Eric Schultz, a senior adviser to Mr. Obama, said in a statement, adding that the president’s strategy was “focused on maximizing his impact, especially where his voice can help move the needle in support of the next generation of leaders.”

Mr. Trump, who is set to speak in Perry, Ga., on Saturday evening, has been pressing a message that Democrats are dangerous extremists who will transform America. He has urged voters to pretend he is on the ballot, hoping to activate his party’s base. But polls show his approval ratings have plummeted, and Republicans are on the defensive over high prices.

At a rally in Florida on Friday, Mr. Trump falsely accused Democrats of being communists and said a vote for Republicans would be a vote for “more money in your pockets, bigger paychecks for your families, lower taxes” and less crime.

The presidents have recently exchanged public criticisms — though Mr. Trump’s have been more frequent, forceful and direct. At a rally in Kansas on Monday, Mr. Trump said Mr. Obama had been a “rotten president.”

Mr. Trump, who succeeded Mr. Obama in office in 2017, had for years promoted a racist, baseless conspiracy theory that Mr. Obama was not born in the United States.

Mr. Obama has been selective about publicly criticizing Mr. Trump by name. Recently, he has expressed disapproval of Mr. Trump’s approach to artificial intelligence, among other topics.

Mr. Obama, who has been out of office for nearly a decade, has engaged heavily with midterm races, taping dozens of ads for candidates. But until now his time on the trail has been limited to some light campaigning in the spring with James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Texas.

On Saturday, Mr. Obama will start in Cleveland with former Senator Sherrod Brown of Ohio, a Democrat who is challenging Senator Jon Husted, a Republican, in one of the country’s most closely watched races. Mr. Obama will also speak in support of Dr. Amy Acton, the Democratic nominee for Ohio governor.

Dr. Acton’s race has consumed national politics in recent days, after her Republican opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy, aired an ad featuring Dr. Acton’s mother, who has been estranged from her daughter for decades. The ad has split Republicans.

Mr. Obama was the last Democratic presidential candidate to carry Ohio, which was once seen as a quintessential swing state but has been drifting toward Republicans for years. But Democrats have grown increasingly confident about their chances there in the November elections.

Mr. Obama will travel next to Detroit to rally with Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the progressive Democratic nominee in Michigan’s pivotal Senate race. Dr. El-Sayed has been trying to shore up his support from Black voters in a contest that Republicans see as their best chance to flip a Senate seat.

In the evening, Mr. Trump will make his appearance in Georgia, a state that Mr. Obama plans to visit later in the week. On Sunday, Mr. Trump is set to visit Michigan.

Mr. Trump has directly addressed Mr. Obama’s trip to Michigan in his own recent remarks and has reminded audiences that he won Michigan in 2016 and 2024.

Mr. Obama has challenged Mr. Trump over his policies. Last month, he publicly criticized Mr. Trump over his approach to A.I. for the first time, warning that the technology could “deeply affect our health and our safety.”

“There’s no replacement for an effective, government regulatory structure,” Mr. Obama said at an event in upstate New York. “And the challenge we have is that, obviously, we have a president currently that has said that’s for losers.”

Last weekend, Mr. Obama also denounced the Trump administration’s intensifying investigation into Representative Ilhan Omar, a Minnesota Democrat, writing on social media that it was “appalling.”

On Saturday, Mr. Obama will also focus on Democratic candidates’ personal stories, his representatives said. Dr. El-Sayed, a son of Egyptian immigrants who would be the first Muslim senator, has been facing attacks from Republicans who say he is ungrateful or disloyal to the United States. Dr. El-Sayed has responded that he believes America represents a “deep and profound” gift.

Mr. Obama, the first Black president, spoke by phone with Dr. El-Sayed soon after he won a divisive primary in August.

item.title: Why Democrats Could Find It Hard to Win the Senate Despite Their Strong Polls
item.description:
Democrats have a hefty advantage in national polls. President Trump is playing defense, campaigning through deep-red corners of the country that he won by overwhelming margins just two years ago. And assumptions that Democrats will win control of Congress have become conventional wisdom in many quarters, from longtime political observers to social media to the oddsmakers in prediction markets.

But as Democratic dreams of midterm victories grow bigger, some strategists quietly worry that expanding expectations are crowding out signs of a more challenging political reality.

Control of the Senate hinges on victories in red states that favored Mr. Trump by significant margins in 2024, including some that Democrats have not won in decades. Republicans are outspending them by eye-popping amounts in key races. And after its performance in 2024, the Democratic Party as a brand still remains unpopular among voters.

All of that has left some in both parties wondering: Could the much-discussed blue wave end up looking more like a splash?

Strategists in both parties believe it is increasingly unlikely that Republicans will be able to hold on to their House majority. But among Democratic donors, activists and voters, hopes of winning control of both chambers have grown so high that some fear any other result could feel like falling short.

“I am concerned that we have an overheating of expectations,” said Molly Murphy, a pollster who worked on the 2024 campaigns of former President Joseph R. Biden Jr. and former Vice President Kamala Harris. “People often assume in a wave you win everything, and what happens in a modern wave is you win far more than normal.”

The kind of broad wins that once defined wave elections are largely a thing of the past, Ms. Murphy said, destroyed by gerrymandering that has left relatively few House seats truly competitive.

In 2018, the most recent midterm election considered a landslide election, Democrats won 41 House seats and control of the chamber. But Republicans gained two Senate seats and expanded their majority.

This year, there’s near-universal agreement among politicians, strategists and activists that Republicans face steeper political headwinds than Democrats. Mr. Trump’s approval rating hit a new low this week, views of the economy are dismal and Democrats lead by 11 points on the generic ballot — a measure often used to gage a party’s strength.

The sharp deterioration of the national political environment for Republicans has transformed the electoral map, forcing their candidates on the defensive in surprising places. This week, Senate Majority PAC, the main super PAC for Senate Democrats, began airing $1.2 million in television ads in Mississippi — a state that hasn’t elected a Democratic U.S. senator since 1982.

That’s a striking reversal of expectations from two years ago, when Democrats began plotting a midterm strategy and winning control of the Senate seemed nearly impossible. Then, Republicans — and some Democrats — scoffed when Senator Chuck Schumer, the minority leader from New York, publicly discussed recruiting a Democratic candidate for Senate in Mississippi.

The question is whether the Democrats’ momentum is strong enough to lift their candidates in deep red states to victory. To win control of the Senate, Democrats must flip four Republican-held seats, and keep all of their own.

Of the 10 Senate battleground contests, four feature Republican incumbents: Senators Dan Sullivan of Alaska, Jon Husted of Ohio, Susan Collins of Maine and Roger Marshall of Kansas. And five are happening in states that Mr. Trump won by 11 points or more in 2024.

“Structurally, the Senate is built to be Republican, and the question is whether this wave can breach that levee,” said Liam Donovan, a Republican strategist. “It is incredibly hard.”

Polling, early-voting turnout and the results of recent special elections suggest that Democrats are far more enthusiastic than Republicans this election cycle.

But those measures, particularly early-vote returns, can be misleading. Turnout can flip on Election Day, particularly if Republicans successfully leverage their campaign war chest and Mr. Trump’s tour through Republican strongholds to drive their supporters to the polls.

“Trump is probably going to do some good in these red-leaning states when he comes in,” said David Kochel, a veteran Republican political strategist from Iowa, where Mr. Trump held a campaign rally on Thursday. “There’s still a lot more Republicans in Iowa and Kansas than there are Democrats.”

In Sioux City, Iowa, on Thursday night, Mr. Trump offered plenty of MAGA red meat, attacking Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, and urging Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate for governor in Ohio, not to take down an ad featuring the estranged mother of his opponent that has drawn bipartisan backlash. And, Mr. Trump told the crowd, he had the “right” to run for a third term.

“I’m asking you to pretend I’m running,” he said, repeating a frequent refrain. “Pretend I’m on the ballot.”

This year, as in several recent election cycles, Democrats harbor considerable anxiety about the accuracy of polling. Some strategists worry that pollsters are oversampling Democrats, particularly in red states, who may be more likely to respond to questions about the election.

A historical assessment of congressional polls conducted by The Economist this week found that the more partisan a state, the more the polls have underestimated the strength of the dominant party.

If that trend held true this year, it would temper Democratic expectations in states like Alaska, Texas, Ohio, Iowa and Kansas.

And even if the polls favoring Democrats turn out to be accurate, many individual Senate races are quite close, in some cases within the margin of error.

“There will be two explanations if the wave is just a ripple,” said Howard Wolfson, a veteran Democratic strategist. “One is there is a massive polling error. The second is that the Democrats didn’t have enough money to put enough races into play and make the races that were in play sufficiently competitive.”

Republicans currently have an advantage of about $650 million in general-election advertising, according to a review of past and future ad reservations across federal and state races by AdImpact, a media-tracking firm.

Their edge is most pronounced in the Senate: In the seven races that the Cook Political Report rated as tossups, Republicans are outspending Democrats on advertising by more than $320 million, according to a separate tally by AdImpact.

The lack of Democratic funds limits the party’s ability to mount aggressive campaigns in the kind of districts that would fuel a wave, said Mr. Wolfson, a political adviser for Michael R. Bloomberg, the former mayor of New York City, who spent about $80 million bolstering Democrats this fall.

So far, the polls haven’t shown significant shifts since more money started pumping into races.

But the spending is being felt not only in the barrage of campaign ads, said Jason Roe, a Republican strategist based in Michigan, but also in efforts to push Republican voters to the polls. Republicans have embraced a version of the strategy that helped them capture the White House in 2024, focusing on driving loyal Republican voters who typically skip midterm elections to the polls.

And just as in 2024, they have gotten plenty of outside help, including from Elon Musk, who has quietly funneled more than $276 million into building a huge turnout operation to help Republicans.

The impact of that work might not be clear until Election Day.

“I have never seen more money spent on the ground in my life — it is obscene,” Mr. Roe said. “If you are a Republican voter, you are going to get harassed to no end to turn out.”

He added: “The question is: How many of those people are so unhappy with Trump or Republicans that they don’t vote for us when they get there?”

Some Democrats also worry that their party’s still-battered brand could hurt their support in November. Even as Democratic candidates gain support, polling shows lingering disapproval of their party overall.

Just 28 percent of voters said they are satisfied with the Democratic Party, in the recent New York Times/Siena poll, eight points lower than satisfaction with the Republican Party and the share of voters who approve of Mr. Trump’s job performance.

Republicans have tried to capitalize on that skepticism by casting Democratic candidates as far-left radicals who want to turn the country into “a socialist hellscape.”

Matt Bennett, a vice president at Third Way, a centrist think tank that presses for a more moderate Democratic approach, worries that some of the party’s more progressive candidates, including Senate nominees Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Troy Jackson in Maine, are underperforming Democrats competing in traditional red states.

Is there a scenario in which Democrats win in red states but squeak by in blue ones? Mr. Bennett doesn’t rule it out. Midterms, he said, can produce strange results.

“Every single one of the Senate races is on a knife’s edge,” Mr. Bennett said. “The results could be super weird.”

item.title: A New 2028 Poll Finds Vance, Rubio and a Mishmash of Democrats in the Mix
item.description:
Democrats still have significant disagreements about their party’s future direction, even as more of them want the party to move to the center than the left, according to a poll from The New York Times and Siena University. The party’s voters also had no consensus on who their 2028 presidential nominee should be.

Republicans, on the other, hand, want their party to follow President Trump’s lead in 2028 and say they prefer Vice President JD Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio to be their next presidential nominee.

The poll shows that while a meaningful slice of Republicans would like to change direction from Mr. Trump, the party remains much more united than Democrats. Still, Republicans face a generational divide, with far more older voters wanting to stick with the Trump path than their younger compatriots.

Both parties are days away from a midterm election that is likely to serve as an inflection point.

Democrats hope that a backlash to Mr. Trump’s policies will power them to victories deep in parts of the country where Republicans have long prevailed. Republicans, for whom Mr. Trump has been the dominant figure for a decade, are betting on his ability to turn out the party’s base. The president himself has urged Republican voters to pretend he is on the ballot.

Mr. Trump’s lasting grip on his party is clear in the poll: When asked an open-ended question about whom they wanted to be the next G.O.P. presidential nominee, 8 percent of Republicans named him, even though he is constitutionally ineligible.

The New York Times/Siena poll

Oct. 12-19

Based on a New York Times/Siena poll of 1,170 self-identified Democratic primary voters in a poll of 3,494 registered voters nationwide conducted Oct. 12 to 19. Candidates are shown if they received over 2 percent of responses. Figures are rounded.

Jillian Vordick/The New York Times

Democrats had no consensus in the poll about whom they would be most likely to vote for in a presidential primary race.

Those surveyed named more than 20 Democrats — including former President Barack Obama and Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York City, who are both ineligible — as their top choice.

Nearly half of potential Democratic primary voters said they did not know whom they wanted to support for president.

The question asked respondents to volunteer their choice of candidate, rather than providing a list of names. With more than two years until the 2028 election, it can be difficult for people to come up with the names of potential contenders.

Still, the party faces a broader fight over its direction as the midterms conclude and the 2028 presidential race takes shape. About 48 percent of Democrats wanted to see the party move toward the political center, compared with 27 percent who thought it should go to the left. About 21 percent of Democrats said the party should stay where it is.

The chasm is wider among independent voters, whom both parties need to win national elections. Of those, 72 percent thought the Democratic Party should move to the center, compared with just 11 percent who wanted it to shift left.

Younger Democrats are more inclined to want the party to move left, while their elders want to see it move to the middle.

When Democrats were asked in the poll whom they would be most likely to vote for in the 2028 primary race, no candidate received more than 12 percent support.

Two of the best-known potential candidates, former Vice President Kamala Harris and Gov. Gavin Newsom of California, topped the list with 12 percent and 9 percent, respectively. They were followed by some of the party’s other prominent figures: former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg (7 percent), Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York (6 percent) and Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia (4 percent).

No major Democratic candidate has announced a presidential campaign yet, though several potential contenders, including Mr. Newsom, Ms. Harris and Ms. Ocasio-Cortez, have publicly deliberated about the possibility. Mr. Buttigieg has traveled the country stumping for Democratic candidates in the midterms. Mr. Ossoff, who is running for re-election, said during a debate last week that he would serve his full six-year Senate term if re-elected and declared that he had “zero interest in running for president.” (Mr. Obama said similar in 2006.)

Fifteen other Democrats were named by at least two poll respondents as preferred 2028 options. Some of these figures are highly unlikely or ineligible to run, including Mr. Obama; Michelle Obama; Mr. Mamdani (he is ineligible to be president because he was born overseas); Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, who is 85 and has said he does not expect to run again; and Hillary Clinton, the party’s presidential nominee in 2016.

The New York Times/Siena poll

Oct. 12-19

Based on a New York Times/Siena poll of 850 self-identified Republican primary voters in a poll of 3,494 registered voters nationwide conducted Oct. 12 to 19. Candidates are shown if they received over 2 percent of responses. Figures are rounded.

Jillian Vordick/The New York Times

Mr. Vance has widely been seen as the most likely heir to Mr. Trump’s political movement since they won the 2024 election together.

The Times/Siena poll indicates that potential Republican primary voters tend to feel that way, too: Thirty-three percent said they would most likely vote for Mr. Vance in a Republican primary, compared with 23 percent for Mr. Rubio, who has said he will defer to Mr. Vance.

A large majority of Republicans in the poll, 63 percent, said they wanted a continuation of Mr. Trump’s policies. Eight percent went so far as to say that he was their first choice for 2028, even though he cannot run because of term limits.

Eleven other Republicans were named by at least two poll respondents. They included Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida (3 percent), Donald Trump Jr. (1 percent) and Mitt Romney, the party’s 2012 nominee, who broke with Mr. Trump long ago.

The poll suggested that it would be challenging for a Romney-like figure who represents the pre-Trump Republican leadership to win the 2028 primary. Just 34 percent of Republicans said they wanted the party to move in a new direction, away from Mr. Trump.

Independent voters have a different view. More than 80 percent of them want Republicans to move away from Mr. Trump, an indication that the president has lost ground with the voters who often decide battleground elections.
