item.title: Trump Relies on Falsehoods to Cast Doubt on Elections
item.description:
In his second term, President Trump has seldom let a day go by without repeating lies about election results or casting doubt on the country’s voting system.

They are falsehoods that in some cases act as a prelude to actions his administration has taken to intervene in the midterm elections, like preemptively seeking to block election results in Alaska should the Republican incumbent narrowly lose or suing California over its voter rolls.

Mr. Trump has only ramped up his attacks as the midterms near and as control of Congress hangs in the balance. He has amplified conspiracy theories about how votes are cast and how they are counted in various states and baselessly declared past election results fraudulent, paving the way for him to question the integrity of the November election.

Here’s a guide to some recent claims.

What Was Said

False. Alaska voters approved a ranked-choice voting system in a 2020 ballot initiative. There is no “guy sitting behind a table just picking a winner.” Rather, voters rank candidates by order of preference. There is no evidence that the system benefits one party over the other.

Under a ranked-choice voting system, voters select their favorite candidate and can indicate their second and subsequent choices. If one candidate receives a majority of first-choice votes, that candidate wins outright. But if no candidate achieves a majority, the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated, and the ballots of voters who ranked that candidate first are then reallocated to their next choice. The process repeats until someone receives a majority of votes.

Asked for evidence that ranked-choice voting was a Democratic “scam,” the White House cited Democrats’ winning House elections in Alaska in 2022 and Maine in 2018.

But in the 2022 election, Alaska voters also used the system to elect a Republican senator and a Republican governor. Two years later, voters used the system to select Mr. Trump and a Republican representative.

The 2018 election in Maine was one of four recent elections in which a candidate in second place in the first round of voting ultimately won after candidates with fewer votes were eliminated. While the victor in that race was a Democrat, two other elections were won by Republicans and another by a Democrat, according to a tally by FairVote, a nonpartisan electoral reform group.

Some research and polls show that Mr. Trump would have been a more likely beneficiary of ranked-choice voting in both the 2020 and 2024 elections, as voters who cast ballots for third-party candidates preferred him to the Democratic nominees.

Ranked-choice voting is still relatively uncommon in American elections, and efforts to expand it may have stalled in recent years. But Mr. Trump is wrong that “everyone is repealing it.”

More than a dozen states, largely Republican strongholds, have banned ranked-choice voting since 2022, but voters in jurisdictions where it is already in place have also rejected efforts to repeal it. Currently, two states (Alaska and Maine) and the District of Columbia use ranked-choice voting for federal and state elections and about three dozen cities use it for local elections.

In 2024, Alaska voters voted to retain ranked-choice voting, as did voters in Bloomington, Minn. Voters in four states did reject efforts to switch to ranked-choice voting, and Missouri banned the practice, but three cities adopted it.

What Was Said

False. Mr. Trump’s baseless election claims have long zeroed in on Arizona. At a recent rally, he again repeated a long-debunked falsehood about the 2022 midterm election in the state.

On Election Day in 2022, technical glitches disrupted the vote counting, but not the ballot-marking process. The glitches affected tabulation machines, which optically scan and count ballots in lieu of hand-counting, in 71 of 223 voting centers in Maricopa County, Ariz.

Two county officials, both Republicans, said on social media that voters could still drop their ballots in a secure box and officials would take their ballots to a central tabulation center later that night. The officials emphasized in a news conference that day that “everyone is still getting to vote,” that “none of this indicates any fraud” and that the secure box option was a “fail safe that functions the exact same way as early voting.”

Officials reported later that day that they had identified the cause of the glitch: Some printers were not producing dark-enough markings on ballots. According to the county’s post-election analysis, the issue had been resolved at most sites by midafternoon and, overall, about 16,700 ballots were affected.

A judge did deny a Republican Party request to keep the polls open for three additional hours, noting that there was no evidence that anyone had been unable to vote.

Kari Lake, the Republican candidate for governor, filed a lawsuit against the county disputing her loss, arguing in part that the glitches were caused intentionally and resulted in a change in outcome. But a state judge ruled that Ms. Lake produced no evidence supporting that assertion. An appeals court upheld that ruling, and the state’s supreme court denied her appeal request.

What Was Said

False. It is rare but not unprecedented for the party in control of the White House to retain or expand control of one chamber of Congress in the midterm elections. In Mr. Trump’s first term and two other instances, the party lost the presidency in the next general election. In three other instances, the party retained it.

The Republican Party lost 40 seats in the House of Representatives in the 2018 midterms, but gained two in the Senate (whether that is a “tremendous” gain is a matter of opinion). Mr. Trump then lost his re-election bid in 2020.

In the 1998 midterm election, Democrats gained five House seats and retained control of the Senate, with no net change in the balance of the upper chamber. Vice President Al Gore then lost the 2000 presidential election.

In the 2022 midterm election, Democrats lost nine House seats and gained one seat in the Senate. Vice President Kamala Harris then lost the 2024 presidential election. By Mr. Trump’s logic, Ms. Harris’s loss, too, should have been “impossible.”

The Democrats lost seats in the House and gained seats in the Senate in the 1914 and 1962 midterm elections, and retained control of the White House in the 1916 and 1964 general elections. Republicans lost seats in the House and gained two seats in the Senate in the 1970 general election, and President Richard Nixon won his re-election campaign in 1972.

What Was Said

False. For months, Mr. Trump has long cited slow counting in the Los Angeles mayoral primary in June — and California in general — as evidence of election fraud, while embellishing details. But a candidate lagging in the initial count and then pulling ahead as more votes are tallied occurs quite often in races, including in elections in which Mr. Trump was a candidate. There is no evidence that the primary was “rigged.”

In recent elections, California has been one of the slowest states to count results. That is in part because it is the most populous but largely because of its counting process.

California relies heavily on mail-in ballots, which delays vote counting as officials verify signatures and give voters the chance to correct discrepancies. Ballots can also be counted if they are postmarked by Election Day and received within seven days, and officials have 30 days to count votes.

In the June mayoral primary in Los Angeles, the first batch of votes counted after polls closed showed Mayor Karen Bass leading with more than 117,000 votes, the reality TV star Spencer Pratt in second with about 86,000 votes and a member of the Los Angeles City Council, Nithya Raman, in third with nearly 62,000 votes. Mr. Pratt maintained his lead over Ms. Raman as more votes were counted on election night.

Ms. Raman spoke at about 11 p.m., when her vote count stood at over 81,000 compared with nearly 142,000 ballots for Ms. Bass and nearly 114,000 for Mr. Pratt. Toward the end of her speech, she began tearing up as she thanked her parents, in-laws, husband and children for their support and patience. She did not concede defeat and instead noted that “tonight may not give us a final answer on this race” and that “many thousands of votes will be counted in the days ahead.”

Mr. Pratt remained in second place for a few days as more votes were counted, but his lead began to narrow and Ms. Raman pulled ahead five days later. In the end, Ms. Bass and Ms. Raman advanced to the general election with 34 percent and 29 percent of the vote. Mr. Pratt, a Republican, received about 25 percent of the vote, which was comparable to Mr. Trump’s own vote share in the city in the 2024 election.

This development was not a surprise to local political observers, who noted that Ms. Raman’s younger progressive supporters tended to vote later than older conservatives who cast their ballots early or in person. Others have noted that Mr. Pratt’s third-place finish and vote share were nonetheless impressive for a first-time candidate in a very liberal city.

item.title: ‘He’s Not the Same Baby’: Family of Child Found Alive in Morgue Recalls Ordeal
item.description:
The mother of a toddler who was pronounced dead at an Arizona hospital in February, then found to be alive hours later in a morgue, is speaking out about her family’s ordeal and raising questions about the care her son received that night.

The mother, Alexus Fiordilino, said in an interview this week that she, her husband and her mother-in-law were at the hospital saying their final goodbyes to her son, Vincent, who was 18 months old at the time, when they thought that maybe “he was trying to breathe.” He had been found unresponsive in a backyard swimming pool hours earlier.

“As I was hugging him,” she said, “air came out of him.”

When they told a police officer and a member of the hospital’s medical staff that Vincent appeared to be exhaling, they were told that it was “agonal breathing,” or “the final death breath,” Ms. Fiordilino said.

“That’s what they confirmed with us over and over,” she added, referring to the medical staff at Dignity Health Mercy Gilbert Medical Center in Gilbert, Ariz., a suburb southeast of Phoenix.

Eight months later, Vincent is unable to walk, talk, sit up or swallow, and is fed through a G.I. tube, Ms. Fiordilino said.

The family’s lawyer, John B. Brewer, said he planned to file a lawsuit as soon as next week. He contends that if Vincent had continued to receive care over the roughly four hours that he was in the morgue, the effects on his health could have been significantly less severe.

The Gilbert Police Department forwarded the case to the Arizona attorney general’s office for review. A spokesman for the attorney general’s office, Richie Taylor, said in an email that it had not yet decided whether to pursue the case.

In July, the Maricopa County Attorney’s Office announced that Ms. Fiordilino and her husband, Angelo, would not face charges. The office said the family “had multiple childproof locks and safety measures in place, and multiple adults were present in the home, all of whom believed someone was watching the child.”

Scott Holden, a lawyer for the doctor in charge of Vincent’s care, Aryan Toosi, and Abby Kay, a spokeswoman for Dignity Health, said in emails that they could not discuss patient care because of patient privacy laws — and, in Dr. Toosi’s case, because of “pending litigation,” Mr. Holden said.

“Dr. Toosi’s thoughts are with the young patient and family, and he wishes the child continued healing and recovery,” Mr. Holden said. “His commitment to delivering high-quality care has always been rooted in a desire to provide healing, safety and comfort to his community.”

In the early evening of Feb. 8, Vincent wandered out of his parents’ sight during a Super Bowl gathering at the family home in Gilbert and was found floating face down and unresponsive in the family’s backyard pool, according to police reports. It is unknown exactly how long Vincent had been in the water, but the reports note that family members said he might have been in the pool for 10 to 15 minutes before being found.

The Fiordilinos took turns performing CPR until the police and emergency medical workers arrived around 5:40 p.m., according to the police reports. After they failed to revive Vincent, he was taken to the emergency department at Mercy Gilbert Medical Center, where medical workers attempted lifesaving measures.

After several minutes, Dr. Toosi left the area where Vincent was being treated, according to the reports.

Around that time, a nurse said, “I have a pulse.” A police officer who was present went to inform Dr. Toosi, who was talking to Vincent’s parents. Dr. Toosi replied, “Please do your thing and let me do my thing; I went to medical school for a reason,” the reports said.

Dr. Toosi then walked to the room where members of his staff were still performing lifesaving measures and listed aloud the treatments the child had received, noting that Vincent had blood gas levels showing “a pH balance incompatible with life,” according to the reports, which paraphrased Dr. Toosi. The doctor then conducted a final pulse check.

“As long as there are no objections, I’d like to call the time of death,” Dr. Toosi said, according to the reports.

No one spoke up, the reports said, and at 6:20 p.m. Dr. Toosi called the time of death and asked for a moment of silence.

Several minutes later, an officer who was present heard what sounded like “gasping” and asked a nurse about it. The nurse said it was agonal breathing, according to the reports.

Vincent was moved to the morgue between 7:18 p.m. and 7:23 p.m., the reports said. At around 11:30 p.m., an employee of the medical examiner’s office in Maricopa County arrived to retrieve the boy’s body and observed that he was still alive. Vincent was then airlifted to Phoenix Children’s Hospital.

The family believes that the hours in the morgue in which Vincent was left without care contributed to the child’s current health outcomes, according to Mr. Brewer.

Ms. Fiordilino and her lawyer said in the interview that Vincent, now 2, would require lifelong care.

“He can understand his name, but that’s kind of it,” Ms. Fiordilino said. “He’s not the same baby.”

Before the accident, Vincent was “very rambunctious,” Ms. Fiordilino said. “He loved to climb on everything,” she added.

“He used to say ‘hi’ all over the place,” she said. “And he had actually just learned ‘bye’ right before this. So I heard him say ‘bye’ one time.”

Mark Walker contributed reporting and Sheelagh McNeill contributed research.

item.title: Trump Asked Muslim Voters to Trust Him. Now Some Feel Used.
item.description:
This month alone, President Trump has called Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan, a “vicious, violent jihadist.” He has repeatedly vilified Somali Americans in Minnesota, prompting calls for security measures at mosques. He gave a lift on Air Force One to a far-right activist who has called herself a proud Islamophobe.

Mr. Trump’s words and actions have rattled communities around the country, including Somali American neighborhoods in Minnesota and predominantly Arab American areas in Michigan. And they have come as anti-Muslim rhetoric has become increasingly normalized in the ranks of the Republican Party ahead of the midterm elections.

For some Muslim voters who backed Mr. Trump in 2024, it all feels like a betrayal.

Two years ago, as a presidential candidate, Mr. Trump made considerable efforts to win votes in some Muslim communities. Now they say that Mr. Trump pledged his support only when it was politically convenient, then alienated and scapegoated them once he won the election.

“My whole community is scared,” said Hassan Nehme, who served as a vice chair to the Michigan Republican Party in 2024 and helped the Trump campaign reach Muslim and Arab American communities like Dearborn. “It’s post-911 in Dearborn. It’s that feeling, like we’re under attack.”

He added: “And this is the same guy we went out and fought tooth and nail for.”

Olivia Wales, a White House spokeswoman, said in a statement that Mr. Trump was “calling out the radical extremists stoking division, defrauding their communities and perpetuating violence.”

She added: “The president will continue to unapologetically fight for American greatness and call out the extremists who want only to divide and destroy.”

Mr. Trump’s allies often respond to criticism of his remarks on Muslims by pointing to the administration’s work securing a cease-fire between Israel and Hamas in Gaza. (The shaky agreement has not stopped Israel from entrenching further into Palestinian territory.)

But the administration has at times appeared to celebrate the reduction in illegal and legal immigration, if it is from a Muslim-majority country.

An official White House social media account has boasted about such declines in “legal immigration from Majority-Muslim Nations.”

But the concerns among Muslims could resonate in next month's elections, even though Mr. Trump is not on the ballot.

A Washington Post-Schar School poll released this week found that 58 percent of registered Arab American voters support Democrats for Congress this year, compared to 34 percent who prefer Republicans, a shift for a group that split its votes between Mr. Trump and former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024.

About half of Arab Americans are Muslim, according to the poll.

Mr. Trump has disparaged Muslims since his first run for president.

He once claimed that Islam “hates us.” During his first run for the White House, he proposed creating a national registry of Muslims. And he carried out a ban on Muslim-majority countries in his first term.

During his 2024 campaign, however, Mr. Trump made a play for these voters, particularly in Michigan, a key battleground with many Arab American and Muslim voters. Mr. Trump sought voters who were unhappy with Democrats over the war in Gaza and other issues, and their support helped lift him to a second term.

After his victory, Mr. Trump promised at one point to stand with Muslim communities. “The Muslim community was there for us in November, and while I’m president, I’m going to be there for you,” Mr. Trump said. “I think you know that.”

The sentiment did not last.

Earlier this month on Air Force One, Mr. Trump hosted Laura Loomer, the right-wing activist who describes Islam as a “cancer” and has posted on social media under the hashtag “#proudislamophobe.”

After giving her a lift to a campaign event, Mr. Trump praised Ms. Loomer as a “great Republican strategist.” She later said on social media that she warned Mr. Trump about the “Islamic takeover infiltrating our government,” and urged him to target Islam more often when speaking about Democrats. In an interview, Ms. Loomer said Mr. Trump appeared “receptive,” adding that she also told Mr. Trump his so-called Muslim ban in his first administration remained popular with his base.

David Campbell, a Notre Dame professor who researches religion and politics, said Mr. Trump was again surfacing anti-Islam sentiment in order to stir up his base, push his supporters to vote and mitigate Democratic gains in November.

“It’s certainly instilling fear,” Mr. Campbell said. “You know, midterm elections are largely about turnout, so they’re clearly trying to turn out the base.”

He said the current climate was a departure for a party once led by President George W. Bush, who in the wake of the Sept. 11 attacks visited a mosque and proclaimed “Islam is peace,” an apparent attempt to quell Islamophobia.

But Mr. Trump’s strategy has also made Muslims in the United States feel like a target, including those who turned to Mr. Trump in 2024 after growing frustrated with the Biden administration on social issues and its foreign policy in the Middle East.

“Donald Trump, for all his flaws, can be a gifted communicator, and knows how to dial it up or dial it down when it’s advantageous to him,” said Fayrouz Saad, a former Biden administration official who helps lead an organization analyzing Muslim and Arab voter data. “And so he saw that opportunity in 2024, and took it.”

“He’s just dialing it up now,” she added.

Mr. Nehme, a Muslim, military veteran and Republican candidate for local office in Michigan, said he was one of many Dearborn residents in 2024 who trusted Mr. Trump.

But over a potluck at his mother-in-law’s home in Dearborn on a recent morning this month, he found himself at a loss for words when his cousin asked him what he thought about Mr. Trump calling Dr. El-Sayed “Mohamed.”

Earlier this week, Mr. Trump said he had called Dr. El-Sayed that because “I just felt like it,” not because he knew it was his middle name.

“Somebody said, ‘How did you do that?’ I said, ‘I’m the president. I can call him whatever the hell I want,’” Mr. Trump said. “And then they sent me his full name, and actually his middle name is Mohamed, you can believe it?”

“One good thing: If you call somebody from that part of the world Mohamed, you’re about 65 percent sure to get it right,” he added.

Mr. Nehme said the story made him question why he had helped the Trump campaign.

“What’s the point if my own party is going to play against us?” he said. “Since I got into the party, it’s constantly been: We’re trying to change the image of the Republican Party from this racist old rich white man image that it has, and I mean every time we’ve gotten there, it’s like they don’t want to.”

Bishara Bahbah, who led the Arab Americans for Trump coalition in 2024, said the president’s comments had cost him Arab and Muslim voters he had previously won over.

“We’ve been fooled. We’ve been taken for fools, and they got our votes,” Mr. Bahbah said. “It’s not just Michigan — it’s throughout the United States. I think the administration has managed to alienate the Arab and Muslim communities, and they will not vote Republican.”

Mr. Trump has been particularly harsh in his rhetoric with the Somali American community in Minneapolis, which is heavily Muslim. Seizing on a welfare fraud scandal that was concentrated among Minnesota’s Somali community, Mr. Trump has disparaged the Somali community as “garbage” who should “go back to where they came from.”

Residents there were particularly alarmed after Mr. Trump said that Minnesota was “being taken over by Somali immigrants,” and that the “people of Minnesota must fight back.” The post came after a spree of shootings that local authorities connected to Somali American gangs.

“The problem we’re facing right now is that every time the president says something, it absolutely emboldens the craziest people in our community,” said Jaylani Hussein, the head of the Minnesota chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations.

Local imams in the community gathered for a meeting after the social media rant and expressed concern over the safety of their mosques.

“These words are reckless,” Imam Abdulahi Farah said at a news conference earlier this month with other Muslim faith leaders in Minneapolis. “They are dangerous, and they have consequences.”

Mr. Farah is an imam at a mosque where a militia group leader who claimed to want to drive Muslims out of the United States set off a bomb in 2017.

“We know what it means when an entire community who comes to worship are made to feel unsafe,” Mr. Farah said. “Blaming an entire community is not accountability. Scapegoating is not a public safety strategy.”

item.title: El-Sayed Needs Black Voters in Michigan. Tensions With Arab Americans Make That Harder.
item.description:
Dr. Abdul El-Sayed will welcome former President Barack Obama to Michigan on Saturday, as the Democratic nominee for Senate seeks to address one of his greatest challenges this year: consolidating support among Black voters.

Dr. El-Sayed is not just managing residual frustrations from a heated primary, in which Black voters overwhelmingly backed his opponent. He is also confronting age-old animosities between the state’s Black and Arab communities.

And he knows it.

“For too many Black Detroiters, in particular, their experience with somebody who looks like me is not a good one,” Dr. El-Sayed, a former public health official who would be America’s first Muslim senator, said this week on a podcast hosted by The Root, a media outlet aimed at Black audiences.

“You go into a gas station and you go to a party store, you’re being talked at from behind bulletproof glass,” he said. “You’re a woman, you’re being catcalled. If you’re a kid, you’re being sold a loosie” — a single cigarette — “out the back.”

Dr. El-Sayed’s blunt description of some of the tensions between Arab business owners and Black residents in Detroit and beyond revealed the racial unease simmering just beneath the surface that is shaping the race.

One recent incident drew widespread attention: A car crash in September involving two women, one Arab American and the other Black, led to confrontation, allegations of a hate crime and a viral video. In another incident, a valet owner was accused of writing an anti-Black racial slur and charged with a hate crime.

“These are relationships in the community for years in this city,” said Mary Waters, a prominent Black city councilwoman in Detroit who has pointedly not endorsed Dr. El-Sayed. “It is because of — maybe not anything to do with him personally — but the Middle Eastern community in general.”

In the primary, Dr. El-Sayed decisively lost Black areas of Detroit to Representative Haley Stevens, whose supporters ran a heavy rotation of ads featuring Mr. Obama’s praise of her work on the 2009 auto industry bailout. Ms. Stevens won majority-Black precincts in Detroit by a 34-percentage-point landslide.

Against this backdrop, the Republican nominee, Mike Rogers, who is white, has been trying to break the traditional Democratic stranglehold on Detroit, the most populous majority-Black city in the country.

On one recent day in the city, Mr. Rogers was slinging drinks at Desmond’s Elegant Affairs, a social spot with a largely Black clientele. On another, his wife was handing out $10 gift cards for gas. Last weekend, he opened a campaign office on Livernois Avenue, a key strip of Black-owned businesses in Detroit, where aides hung signs and laid out free Domino’s pizzas for the few dozen attendees.

Dr. El-Sayed dismissed Mr. Rogers’s Black outreach as too little, too late.

“That’s cute,” he said in an interview. “How many people are actually from Detroit?” he asked about the crowd.

He also boasted of his own big crowds in the conservative Upper Peninsula, typically more hostile terrain for a Democrat.

“I am making incursions in his base,” Dr. El-Sayed said.

Beneath the bravado has been a flurry of outreach to Black voters.

In the last week, he appeared on The Root’s podcast; did an event with Jemele Hill, a prominent Black journalist; campaigned on Wednesday with Senator Raphael Warnock of Georgia, the pastor of the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.’s old church, Ebenezer Baptist in Atlanta; and spent last Sunday morning visiting two Black churches in Flint with Representative Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts, who sat with clergy leaders and Dr. El-Sayed before services.

On Saturday, Mr. Obama, who won Michigan easily in both 2008 and 2012 and cut an ad in support of Dr. El-Sayed this month, is scheduled to campaign with him. Last month Dr. El-Sayed rolled out a policy agenda specifically aimed at Black communities.

“I’m a cynical Black voter, so I didn’t give Abdul anything,” Ms. Pressley said in an interview on her third day campaigning for him. “I’m here because he made a believer out of me.”

Some in Michigan’s Black community still recall the Uncommitted movement during the 2024 Democratic primary, when members of the Arab American community organized a protest vote against former President Joseph R. Biden Jr. over his support for Israel.

The ill will, stemming from Israel’s war in Gaza, spilled onto former Vice President Kamala Harris when she became the nominee in August of that year. In Dearborn, the city with Michigan’s largest share of Arab American voters, she received less than half the votes Mr. Biden had in 2020.

Ms. Harris campaigned with Dr. El-Sayed last month in Detroit.

But Ms. Waters, the Detroit councilwoman, said that for some Black voters, no surrogate would prove powerful enough to overcome grievances rooted in personal experiences at gas stations and grocery stores.

“Even if she walked down the street with Abdul El-Sayed holding his hand, they would still not vote for him,” Ms. Waters said of Ms. Harris, adding that some Black voters were even drawing on the language of the Uncommitted movement: “People are saying they’re going to ‘leave it blank.’”

Dr. El-Sayed will almost certainly win the Black vote comfortably, but for Democrats to prevail in Michigan, they typically need Black voters to come to the polls in high numbers and to vote overwhelmingly Democratic.

“Rogers has been out in the neighborhoods, and that’s smart,” said Adrian Hemond, a Democrat of mixed race who runs a bipartisan consulting firm in Michigan. “He’s not going to win them, but if he can get in the high teens, low 20s, percentage-wise, with Black men, that’ll go a long way.”

At a Rogers campaign event at a winery in more rural Oakland County, a clutch of Black women surrounded Mr. Rogers and gave him hugs after a speech.

“You guys are the best ever,” Mr. Rogers told them.

“His community, the Arabic community — for so long they have disrespected the Black community,” one of the women, Cynthia Haines of Flint, said about Dr. El-Sayed in an interview. She was excited to vote for Mr. Rogers.

A super PAC called Together for Michigan has created a “Democrats for Rogers” campaign and is running an ad featuring Black voters and leaders.

Melanie Rutherford, 47, a Democrat and former councilwoman in Pontiac, was paid $30,000 last month by the group. Ms. Rutherford, who is Black, was among those at Mr. Rogers’s Detroit office opening, laying her hands on him at one point and leading the room in prayer.

In an interview, Ms. Rutherford called herself a “Haley Stevens fanatic” in the primary, saying she had never voted Republican. But she said she was alienated by the choice of Dr. El-Sayed over Ms. Stevens, who had done a lot for her city, and predicted that Black-Arab tensions would be a factor in November.

“Every liquor store is owned by Arabs — ain’t nothing wrong with that,” she said. “It’s not about the ownership. It’s about the respect.”

Darrell Roper, a 76-year-old Black retiree who lives in Genesee, acknowledged those tensions as he met Dr. El-Sayed in the lobby of Metropolitan Baptist Church in Flint on Sunday. But he said he was eager to support the Democrat to curb President Trump.

“If he helps his people,” Mr. Roper said of Dr. El-Sayed, whose parents are Egyptian immigrants, “it’s going to help us.”

Mr. Rogers is hoping to exploit the opening.

“I’ll tell you one thing — they know that there’s one guy that can help heal that. That’s us,” Mr. Rogers said in an interview at his Detroit office opening. “He cannot heal that.”

But he’s trying everything he can. This month, at a campaign event at a dive bar in Grand Rapids, Dr. El-Sayed took a question from a disillusioned Black voter named JD Chapman Jr.

“What makes you different,” said Mr. Chapman, 46, “and how do we know that we can trust what you say?”

Dr. El-Sayed began, as he often does, by describing the possibility of his own political rise as a direct function of the Black civil rights movement.

“My story in America doesn’t happen without the advocacy and the organizing of Black folks,” he told Mr. Chapman. He cited the immigration law, which came along with better-known civil rights bills of the 1960s, that allowed his father to immigrate here. “So I owe a deep debt of gratitude to Black folk.”

He spoke about tackling racial and health disparities in Detroit and Wayne County as a public health official, about giving away eyeglasses, about putting Narcan in vending machines.

Mr. Chapman was not impressed.

He said in an interview that he did not find Dr. El-Sayed trustworthy or his answers concrete enough. He had voted for Ms. Stevens in the primary but was “very, very seriously considering” not voting for Senate in the general election.

“I’m not sold,” he said.

Evan Reynolds contributed reporting.

item.title: How the Most Ruthless Ad of the Midterms Divided Republicans
item.description:
The most explosive advertisement of the midterm elections has split Republicans and again posed the question of what is fair game for campaign attacks in American politics.

In the days since the leak of the ad from Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for governor of Ohio, many fellow G.O.P. politicians have denounced, disavowed or distanced themselves from the spot. Yet President Trump and Vice President JD Vance have defended the ad, a remarkably ruthless one even by the standards of modern political campaigns.

The ad features the estranged mother of Mr. Ramaswamy’s Democratic opponent, Amy Acton, calling her daughter a liar and urging Ohioans not to vote for her. Ms. Acton has said that she has not spoken to her mother since she was 12 years old, when she was removed from her mother’s custody after her stepfather was arrested and charged with raping her.

The outrage over the ad’s dark backstory has left Mr. Ramaswamy, a billionaire entrepreneur who exemplifies the anything-goes, attack-at-all-costs ethos of Trump-era politics, at the center of a self-created political firestorm.

The Republican disagreements over the ad show that major figures in the party can still become divided over the rules and red lines of political warfare in the Trump era. And they set the stage for high drama on Election Day in Ohio, a state that has trended solidly Republican in recent years but now has outsize importance in the midterms. The overarching political question is: Will a potential backlash to Mr. Ramaswamy hurt other Ohio Republicans in competitive races, especially Senator Jon Husted, who is trying to fend off a well-known Democratic rival in a vital race for Senate control?

There is now a degree of unpredictability in the state. Campaigns in both parties do not know how voters will react.

Mr. Ramaswamy, who along with his aides declined to be interviewed for this article, said at a campaign stop on Friday that he had no regrets. The ad, he suggested, was his attempt to change the rules of engagement for Republicans in Ohio — just as Mr. Trump has done in Washington.

“What we need is a governor at the top just like President Trump is for our country — a governor for this state who stands strong, who says we will not play on your terms,” he told a crowd in Strongsville, a Cleveland suburb. “We will stand for what we know is right and true, and we will not apologize for it.”

There had been rumblings for weeks in Ohio political circles that Mr. Ramaswamy’s top aides were in touch with Dr. Acton’s estranged mother.

Dr. Acton’s troubled childhood was no secret, and had been the subject of reporting during her high-profile stretch as the pandemic-era health director for Gov. Mike DeWine, a Republican.

Mr. Ramaswamy had been trailing Dr. Acton in many public and private polls. Like other Republicans, he was confronting voter frustration with high gas prices, tariffs and Mr. Trump’s leadership.

Producing the ad was a politically hazardous move for Mr. Ramaswamy, a 41-year-old start-up founder who has shown a high tolerance for risk since he emerged on the scene during his 2024 campaign for president. During that race, he presented himself as a full Trump acolyte and made plenty of enemies with his brash style before placing fourth in the Iowa caucuses, dropping out and endorsing Mr. Trump.

The Ramaswamy campaign was still testing the ad to gauge its effectiveness when the spot burst into public view late Monday.

D.J. Byrnes, a left-leaning local journalist known as the Rooster, published the ad online, calling it “loathsome.”

The spot, which took little time to spread widely online, showed Dr. Acton’s 82-year-old mother, Donna Arthur, using harsh language to denounce her estranged daughter.

“Don’t let her become your governor,” Ms. Arthur said.

The backlash was immediate and intense.

As the controversy swirled, Mr. Ramaswamy reached out privately to other Ohio Republicans to gauge their reaction, according to three people briefed on the exchanges. He felt the coverage by the news media was unfair and wanted a chance to explain his thinking, even if it did not lead to public support for running the ad.

Governor DeWine called the ad “deeply, deeply troubling” and “just plain wrong,” and he urged Mr. Ramaswamy — whom he has endorsed — to take it down. Mr. Husted, who faces his own tight election against former Senator Sherrod Brown on Nov. 3, said he would not have run the ad. Republicans in close races in other states, like Representative Ashley Hinson of Iowa, who is running for Senate, said it should come off the air.

Not only has Mr. Ramaswamy so far declined to back away from the ad, but his campaign also bought more than $4 million in Ohio airtime to show it to viewers.

Supporters of Mr. Ramaswamy echoed his contention that he has been treated unfairly by the news media and argued that there had been no public anger when Dr. Acton’s campaign had attacked him.

“Democrats and the media are trying to change the subject from ‘she’s a liar’ to ‘she was abused as a child,’” Beth Lear, an Ohio state representative from just north of Columbus, wrote in an opinion essay published Friday in The Columbus Dispatch. “It’s a masterful attempt to manipulate voters’ emotions by making Amy a victim.”

The ad served as an attempt to shift the focus of the campaign in its final days from frustrations about Mr. Trump’s economy to a referendum on Dr. Acton’s honesty. But in so doing, it placed Mr. Ramaswamy’s own morals and ethics in the spotlight, and reminded voters that Dr. Acton survived a seriously troubled childhood.

Mr. Ramaswamy has, in a sense, run a political psychology experiment on his home state. Will voters in Ohio be outraged that he has tried to secure a political advantage through a woman estranged from her daughter over allegations of rape, or will they better recall the accusation that Dr. Acton is lying?

“We ran an ad about lying,” Mr. Ramaswamy told the crowd in Strongsville. “Amy Acton is lying. She has been lying this entire campaign about me.”

But at a pumpkin festival on Friday night in Circleville, Ohio, Mr. Ramaswamy’s running mate, State Senator Rob McColley, said the campaign did not believe Dr. Acton was lying about her childhood abuse.

“Oh no, that is horrible,” Mr. McColley said. “We are accusing her of lying in her adult career.”

Dr. Acton’s campaign has almost run out of words to express its disgust over the ad. A spokeswoman, Addie Bullock, has called it “despicable,” “disturbing” and “disqualifying.”

“Ramaswamy will do anything, including embrace child sex predators, to get what he wants,” Ms. Bullock said.

Court documents from Mahoning County, Ohio, back up the descriptions by Dr. Acton and her brother of the events of her childhood. In 1978, when Dr. Acton was 12, her stepfather, Cledith Arthur, was arrested and charged with raping her.

He pleaded not guilty and was indicted by a grand jury, after which Ms. Arthur lost custody of Dr. Acton and her brother. A month later, court records show, Mr. Arthur fled the area, and a warrant was issued for his arrest. The Arthurs appear to have lived the ensuing decades in Pennsylvania, and according to Dr. Acton’s brother, they stayed together until Mr. Arthur died in 2004.

In the campaign ad, Ms. Arthur accuses her daughter of lying about her past but does not address the rape allegations.

It is not clear where Ms. Arthur lives now, and she did not respond to messages this week.

She had been living in her car with some cats in the Calvary Church parking lot, just outside Boalsburg, Pa., according to the Rev. Stacy Sublett, the church’s pastor. Mr. Sublett said that he had tried to find Ms. Arthur permanent housing in the area but that she declined the assistance.

He said he was not aware of friends or family who came to see her.

Jessica Contrera contributed reporting from Akron, Ohio, David DeKok from Boalsburg, Pa., and Kevin Williams from Circleville, Ohio. Kitty Bennett contributed research.
